meta.abstract: Soitec SA (Euronext Paris: SOI) is the world's dominant manufacturer of engineered semiconductor substrates, holding an effective monopoly in fully depleted silicon-on-insulator (FD-SOI) and radio-frequency SOI (RF-SOI) wafers through its proprietary Smart Cut™ ion-implantation-and-bonding process, which it has commercialised since its 1992 founding by CEA-Leti researchers André-Jacques Auberton-Hervé and Jean-Michel Lamure in Bernin, France. The company's core thesis rests on three interlocking structural tailwinds: (1) the progressive migration of 5G and nascent 6G RF front-end modules from bulk silicon to SOI and piezoelectric-on-insulator (POI) substrates, where Soitec has secured long-term volume agreements with Qualcomm and MediaTek for its Bernin and Singapore fabs; (2) the proliferation of FD-SOI as the preferred node for ultra-low-power edge AI chips and automotive ADAS processors, where the substrate's back-biasing capability confers a density-per-watt advantage that bulk CMOS cannot easily replicate at equivalent cost; and (3) the emergent SmartSiC™ silicon carbide platform targeting EV power electronics, a market segment now facing a near-term headwind from Chinese entrant pricing pressure that forced a €41 million asset impairment in the first half of fiscal year 2026. The dossier examines Soitec at a pivotal inflection: fiscal year 2025 revenue declined 8.9 percent to €891 million following a 2024 inventory correction in mobile, H1 FY2026 fell a further 29 percent year-on-year to €231 million, and the company executed a high-profile CEO transition—Pierre Barnabé departing after nearly a decade, succeeded on 1 April 2026 by Laurent Rémont, a 54-year-old Infineon Technologies and STMicroelectronics veteran whose RF and sensors expertise maps directly onto Soitec's core revenue streams. Against this cyclical trough, the group retains a fortress balance sheet (net debt €94 million, equity €1.6 billion as of March 2025) and a medium-term revenue ambition of $2 billion at roughly 40 percent EBITDA margin, underpinned by Singapore capacity doubling to two million 300 mm-equivalent wafers per year and a defended IP portfolio of several hundred Smart Cut–related patents.

chapters.title: The Substrate Monopolist at the Trough: Soitec's Strategic Position in May 2026
chapters.body:
## A Monopoly at the Bottom of the Cycle

Few companies in the semiconductor supply chain occupy so singular a position as Soitec. The Bernin, Isère-based substrate maker holds a near-monopoly on the production of silicon-on-insulator wafers through its Smart Cut™ process — a hydrogen-ion-implantation and molecular-bonding technique co-invented by its founders at the CEA-Leti laboratory in Grenoble and protected by a patent estate refreshed at roughly eighteen new filings per year for three decades. No foundry, no commodity silicon producer, and no venture-backed entrant has replicated the process at commercial yield and scale. That technological singularity is the central fact of any investment or strategic analysis of the company, because it means the current revenue trough — real, painful, and prolonged — is a cyclical correction imposed on an intact structural franchise, not a sign that the franchise itself is eroding.

That distinction matters acutely in May 2026. Soitec's revenue peaked at [€1.09 billion in FY2023](https://www.soitec.com/docs/default-source/financial-reports/2024-2025/en/soitec-fy25-results-presentation.pdf) (the fiscal year ending 31 March 2023), driven by the 5G smartphone supercycle that pulled through record volumes of RF-SOI and early POI wafers. Two years of inventory destocking and handset-unit softness across the mobile supply chain reduced full-year FY2025 revenue to [€890.85 million](https://www.soitec.com/docs/default-source/financial-documents/2024-2025/en/en---q4-revenue-full-year-results---2024-2025---2025-05-27.pdf), an 8.9 percent decline year-on-year, itself following a 10.2 percent drop in FY2024. The trailing twelve months through September 2025 came in at approximately €784 million — a nearly 28 percent contraction from the peak.

| Period | Revenue (€m) | Change YoY |
|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | 862.7 | — |
| FY2023 (peak) | 1,090.0 | +26% |
| FY2024 | 977.9 | −10.2% |
| FY2025 | 890.9 | −8.9% |
| TTM (to Sept 2025) | ~784 | — |

What the revenue decline does not show is a margin collapse. EBITDA margins held above 33 percent through the down-cycle — 33.5 percent on the FY2025 full year, 34.1 percent in the first half of FY2026 — a resilience that reflects the locked-in economics of long-term supply agreements and the absence of spot-price exposure that defines the commodity wafer business. The balance sheet remained conservative: [net debt of €94 million against shareholders' equity of €1.6 billion](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/11/19/3191252/0/en/SOITEC-SOITEC-REPORTS-SECOND-QUARTER-REVENUE-AND-HALF-YEAR-RESULTS-OF-FISCAL-YEAR-2026.html) as of 31 March 2025, with €808 million in cash on hand as of September 2025 — more than enough to absorb the €140 million FY2026 capital expenditure programme and fund the remaining commissioning of the expanded Singapore fab.

## A New CEO Signals a Strategic Recentring

Against that backdrop, the board's appointment of Laurent Rémont as chief executive — effective 1 April 2026, following a brief handover period as special adviser to outgoing CEO Pierre Barnabé — reads as a deliberate signal. Rémont spent six years as Senior Vice President of the Radio Frequency and Sensors division at Infineon Technologies, overseeing MEMS microphones, pressure sensors, and RF switch products before joining Soitec. Before Infineon he spent more than fifteen years at STMicroelectronics, giving him direct exposure to FD-SOI process development from the foundry side. He is, in short, an RF-and-substrate specialist, not a diversification architect.

Barnabé, who led Soitec from 2017 through the revenue scaling from roughly €600 million to the FY2023 peak, announced his departure on 1 October 2025 as the contraction deepened. His successor's profile suggests the board has decided that the path back to growth runs through the core RF, edge AI, and photonics substrate franchises rather than through new material platforms.

## Three Theses, One Open Question

Soitec's medium-term investment case rests on three interlocking narratives that subsequent chapters of this dossier will examine in detail.

The first is the RF substrate upgrade cycle. RF-SOI volumes are directly proportional to 5G handset sell-through and to the escalating complexity of RF front-end modules; the migration from Sub-6 GHz to millimetre-wave and the early architecture work for 6G increases substrate content per phone even at flat unit volumes. POI — Soitec's fastest-growing platform, anchored by a long-term supply agreement with Qualcomm for RF360 module production — compounds this story, as BAW filter proliferation in 5G handsets requires more and higher-quality piezoelectric-on-insulator wafers per device generation.

The second is FD-SOI as the preferred substrate for edge AI and automotive compute. Fully depleted silicon-on-insulator's back-gate biasing capability delivers 30–40 percent lower active power than equivalent bulk CMOS at the 22–28 nm nodes where automotive MCUs, ADAS processors, and industrial inference chips are concentrated — nodes where the economics of a new advanced-node migration are unattractive. The Edge & Cloud AI segment, which includes both FD-SOI and Photonics-SOI, grew 34 percent organically in H1 FY2026 even as Mobile Communications contracted 30 percent.

The third narrative — SmartSiC — remains an open question. The silicon carbide substrate platform received a [€41 million non-current asset impairment charge in H1 FY2026](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/11/19/3191252/0/en/SOITEC-SOITEC-REPORTS-SECOND-QUARTER-REVENUE-AND-HALF-YEAR-RESULTS-OF-FISCAL-YEAR-2026.html), reflecting an accelerated pricing assault by Chinese SiC entrants that compressed the addressable premium for Soitec's bonded-layer approach. The impairment triggered a 28.7 percent single-day share price decline on 20 November 2025, confirming the market's sensitivity to any dilution of Soitec's all-weather margin story.

## From €891 Million to Two Billion

The company's stated medium-term revenue target is $2 billion — approximately €1.85 billion at current exchange rates — with roughly 40 percent EBITDA margin. That ambition implies nearly doubling trough revenue over a five-year horizon, a compound rate requiring the mobile recovery, POI ramp, and edge AI expansion to fire in sequence rather than simultaneously.

The variables are tractable but not trivial. POI volumes depend on Qualcomm and MediaTek executing their RF360 and comparable module roadmaps on schedule and absorbing Singapore output. The RF-SOI recovery requires foundry customers GlobalFoundries and TSMC to rebuild wafer-start orders as handset channel inventory normalises — a process that appeared to be advancing in Q2 FY2026, where sequential volumes rose 47 percent from the Q1 trough. FD-SOI's edge AI upside is real but bounded by the pace at which Samsung Foundry and STMicroelectronics win AI-inference design starts at their respective 28FDS and 22FD-SOI nodes. And the SmartSiC decision — persist, license, or withdraw further — sits squarely in Laurent Rémont's inbox on day one.

What is not in question is the structural position. The Smart Cut moat — technological, economic, and relational — does not erode in a down-cycle. The foundries cannot qualify alternative substrates in under twelve to twenty-four months even if alternatives existed. They do not. Soitec enters 2026 battered in revenue and stock price, but its core franchise is precisely where it was at the peak. That is the thesis: the trough is the entry point, not the warning sign.

chapters.title: From Grenoble Lab to Global Monopoly: Soitec's Thirty-Year Arc
chapters.body:
## The Lab on the Isère

On 27 February 1992, two researchers from the Commissariat à l'Énergie Atomique's Laboratoire d'Électronique et de Technologie de l'Information — known universally in microelectronics circles as CEA-Leti — walked out of its modernist campus in the hills above Grenoble and registered a company in the neighbouring commune of Bernin. André-Jacques Auberton-Hervé, a physicist, and Jean-Michel Lamure, an engineer, named their venture Soitec, a contraction of *silicium sur isolant et technologie*, and its stated purpose was modest to the point of understatement: to commercialise a wafer-transfer process the two men had co-invented with colleagues at the laboratory.

The process, which Soitec would trademark as Smart Cut™, addressed a specific and commercially punishing problem that had bedevilled silicon-on-insulator technology since the 1970s. SOI wafers — in which a thin single-crystal silicon layer is separated from the bulk substrate by a buried oxide — had long been recognised as superior to conventional bulk silicon for high-frequency and low-power integrated circuits. The problem was manufacturing. The prevailing techniques, Separation by Implanted Oxygen (SIMOX) and Bond-and-Etch-back SOI (BESOI), each carried disqualifying defects at commercial volumes. SIMOX produced SOI films with defect densities an order of magnitude too high for advanced logic, while BESOI's mechanical thinning of the donor layer could not achieve the sub-100-nanometre thickness uniformity required for next-generation transistors — nor the throughput a foundry customer ordering tens of thousands of wafers per month needed.

Smart Cut™ resolved both problems through an elegant combination of ion implantation and molecular bonding. A thin layer of hydrogen ions was implanted into a silicon donor wafer at a precisely calibrated depth; the donor was then bonded to an oxidised handle wafer; and a controlled heat treatment caused the implanted layer to cleave along the ion-damaged plane, transferring an atomically smooth silicon film of uniform thickness to the insulating substrate. Crucially, the donor wafer — instead of being consumed by grinding as in BESOI — could be reclaimed and reused, a cost advantage that proved decisive. The resulting SOI film exhibited defect densities comparable to bulk silicon and thickness uniformity achievable at the angstrom level. For the foundry industry shrinking feature sizes toward 90 nm, that combination was transformative.

## The Shin-Etsu Watershed

For its first five years, Soitec was principally a development company, dependent on CEA-Leti for technical support and on European research contracts for operating capital. The strategic inflection came in 1997, when the company concluded a cross-licensing agreement with Shin-Etsu Handotai, Japan's largest silicon wafer producer. Under the arrangement, SEH received a licence to the Smart Cut™ patent portfolio and took an equity stake in Soitec; in exchange, Soitec gained access to SEH's materials expertise and, crucially, a commercial endorsement that reverberated through the Japanese semiconductor industry — then still the world's dominant logic production base — and into the IDMs and foundries in Korea, Taiwan, and the United States who watched Tokyo's standards-setting institutions closely.

The SEH deal also crystallised the business model Soitec would use for the next three decades: license the core IP to qualified partners wishing to manufacture their own SOI wafers, while simultaneously supplying finished wafers directly to foundry and IDM customers under long-term volume agreements. Licensing revenue created a royalty floor and funded ongoing process R&D; the wafer-supply business captured the larger margin opportunity as SOI volumes scaled. It was a model that would prove exceptionally durable.

## IPO, Bernin 1, and the 300-mm Transition

In 1999, on the crest of the first semiconductor capital-expenditure supercycle, Soitec listed on the Paris Nouveau Marché, raising fresh capital that funded the construction of Bernin 1 — by the time of its completion, the largest dedicated SOI wafer manufacturing facility in the world. The timing was fortuitous and then alarming: the dotcom correction of 2000–2001 froze equipment spending across the industry, but SOI's structural advantages for the 130-nm and 90-nm logic generations kept customer qualification activity alive through the trough. A second Bernin production hall followed, and Soitec completed the 200-mm-to-300-mm wafer transition in step with its foundry customers — a technically demanding migration that smaller rivals could not execute without access to the licensing income required to cross-subsidise the capital expenditure.

Through the mid-2000s, the company deepened a collaboration with STMicroelectronics and CEA-Leti on a derivative platform that would become commercially important a decade later: Fully Depleted Silicon-on-Insulator, or FD-SOI, in which an ultra-thin buried oxide layer enables back-gate biasing of the channel region, delivering 30 to 40 percent active-power reduction relative to equivalent bulk-CMOS designs at 28 nm and 22 nm nodes. The first commercial RF-SOI volumes — wafers on high-resistivity substrates destined for switch die in mobile handset RF front-end modules — also ramped in this period, establishing the supply relationships with GlobalFoundries and TSMC that would eventually drive Soitec's revenue above €1 billion.

## The Solar Detour and Its Undoing

Between roughly 2009 and 2015, Soitec pursued one of the more instructive diversification errors in French industrial history. Reasoning that Smart Cut™'s layer-transfer capability could be applied to III-V compound semiconductors as well as silicon, the company built a concentrator photovoltaics business, Soitec Solar GmbH, targeting utility-scale generation with high-efficiency multijunction cells. The technology thesis was coherent; the commercial outcome was not. The cost-per-watt of concentrator PV fell far more slowly than that of conventional crystalline silicon panels, which were simultaneously experiencing a Chinese-manufacturing-driven price collapse. Soitec Solar accumulated losses through the early 2010s and by 2015 was wound down, absorbing write-offs that contributed to several years of negative free cash flow. LED substrates, a parallel diversification pursued through the same period, met a similar fate as conventional architectures proved sufficient without engineered SOI wafers.

The two failures prompted a strategic reorientation under CEO Paul Boudre and, from 2017, Pierre Barnabé: exit all non-SOI activities and concentrate capital entirely on RF-SOI, FD-SOI, and the emerging POI piezoelectric-on-insulator platform. The lesson was filed and not forgotten.

## The Barnabé Era: From €600 Million to Peak

The years from 2017 to 2023 constituted the most commercially successful period in Soitec's history. The 4G-to-5G handset transition proved an extraordinary tailwind for RF-SOI volumes: a 5G Sub-6 GHz smartphone requires more radio bands, more antenna switches, and more low-noise amplifiers than its 4G predecessor, and each function runs on a die manufactured on Soitec's wafers at GlobalFoundries' Malta fab or TSMC's Hsinchu lines. Revenue grew from approximately €600 million at the start of Barnabé's tenure to a peak of €1.09 billion in FY2023.

The Singapore investment was the defining capital commitment of those years. Construction of the expanded Pasir Ris Wafer Fab Park facility began in December 2022, adding roughly 45,000 square metres of cleanroom space with the explicit purpose of doubling annual POI and RF-SOI production capacity to approximately two million 300-mm-equivalent wafers per year. The decision was underwritten by long-term volume agreements with Qualcomm Technologies — a high-volume manufacturing contract for POI wafers destined for Qualcomm's RF360 front-end module production — and with MediaTek. By 2024–2025 the facility was in production ramp, validating Soitec's 5G filter substrate thesis at commercial volumes.

The SmartSiC investment — a Smart Cut™-derived silicon carbide substrate platform targeting EV power electronics — ran a parallel and ultimately unhappier course. The thesis was structurally sound: EV inverter designers needed SiC substrates at cost curves that commodity boule growers were struggling to deliver. But the pace of Chinese SiC entrant pricing pressure in 2024–2025 outran even conservative market forecasts. In November 2025, Soitec recorded a €41 million impairment of SmartSiC non-current assets, a charge that triggered a 28.7 percent single-day decline in the company's share price on 20 November 2025.

## The Rémont Appointment

Barnabé announced his resignation on 1 October 2025, effective 31 March 2026. The board, now chaired by Frédéric Lissalde — the former BorgWarner chief executive appointed chairman in March 2025, bringing automotive electrification experience at a moment of SiC uncertainty — named Laurent Rémont as successor on 8 January 2026. Rémont, a Grenoble INP–ENSERG engineering graduate aged 54 at appointment, had spent six years as Senior Vice President of Infineon Technologies' Radio Frequency and Sensors division, encompassing MEMS microphones, pressure sensors, and RF switch products, and fifteen earlier years at STMicroelectronics across FD-SOI process development and mobile communications customers. He joined Soitec on 16 March 2026 as a special adviser and formally assumed the CEO title on 1 April 2026.

The board's rationale was legible: Rémont's RF semiconductor and MEMS background positioned him to prosecute the 5G/6G filter and edge AI substrate theses that Barnabé had seeded, while his Infineon years gave him credibility with the RF module ecosystem customers — Qualcomm, Murata, TDK-EPCOS — who would determine the pace of POI volume ramp. The strategic question he inherited — whether to persist with SmartSiC, monetise the IP through licensing, or curtail capital commitments further — remained formally unresolved at the frozen-window date of 23 May 2026. What was not in question was the institution he had agreed to run: a company that had spent thirty-four years translating a Grenoble laboratory insight into a near-monopoly over the category of engineered substrate that the RF front-end and edge-AI ecosystems could not yet do without.

chapters.title: The Smart Cut Portfolio: RF-SOI, FD-SOI, POI, SmartSiC, and the Engineered Substrate Platform
chapters.body:
## The Physics of the Cut

At the heart of every Soitec wafer is a process that looks, when described simply, almost too elegant to be real. Smart Cut™ — co-invented by the company's founders while at CEA-Leti in Grenoble and industrialised at Bernin over three decades — begins with a crystalline silicon donor wafer bombarded by hydrogen ions accelerated to a precisely calibrated energy. Those ions implant at a controlled depth below the surface, creating a layer of micro-bubbles — a weakening plane, invisible to the eye but exact to within angstroms — that scribes a parting line into the crystal lattice.

The donor wafer is then bonded face-to-face to a handle wafer — typically a silicon substrate topped with a thermally grown oxide — via molecular adhesion: two polished surfaces brought into contact in a clean-room bond spontaneously through van der Waals and hydrogen forces, without adhesive or heat. Thermal annealing or mechanical cleaving propagates a fracture precisely along the implanted plane, separating the thin transferred layer from the donor bulk. What remains on the handle is an ultra-thin single-crystal film sitting atop a buried oxide, the donor wafer recycled and re-used.

The advantage over grinding or oxidation-based alternatives is uniformity. Grinding introduces sub-micron thickness variation that compounds across a wafer diameter; oxidation-derived films cannot match the crystalline perfection of a transferred single-crystal layer. Smart Cut™ routinely delivers device-layer thickness variation of less than one nanometre across a 300 mm wafer — a specification foundry customers have embedded into process qualifications and that no alternative approach has matched at production scale. The underlying intellectual property, built into a portfolio of several thousand patents with approximately 18 new filings annually, makes Smart Cut™ both a technological moat and a licensing instrument — as the 1997 cross-licensing agreement with Shin-Etsu Handotai, which converted a potential competitor into a minority shareholder, first demonstrated.

## RF-SOI: The Revenue Engine

Radio-frequency silicon-on-insulator is Soitec's largest single revenue contributor and the product line most directly leveraged to the 5G upgrade cycle. The substrate is built on a high-resistivity silicon handle — resistivity typically above 1,000 ohm-cm versus the 10–20 ohm-cm of standard silicon — which minimises parasitic losses at the gigahertz frequencies at which smartphone antenna-switch and low-noise-amplifier circuits operate. Without that high-resistivity foundation, eddy currents induced in the substrate at radio frequencies dissipate signal power and degrade linearity; RF-SOI eliminates the problem at the material level.

The product feeds the switch and LNA die sets manufactured at GlobalFoundries' Fab 9 in Malta, New York, on the 45RFSOI node and its 9SW successor — a dedicated radio-solution platform for which Soitec formalised a supply agreement. TSMC's RF process flows and UMC's RF-CMOS lines also take RF-SOI wafers, supplying Qualcomm, MediaTek, Murata, and Skyworks designs that ship inside virtually every premium Android and Apple handset globally.

The content-per-device story anchors the structural growth argument. A 4G LTE flagship front-end module contains roughly four to six RF switches and two to four LNAs, carrying approximately $0.80–$1.20 of RF-SOI substrate value. A 5G Sub-6 GHz device, with its multi-band carrier aggregation and wider antenna array, lifts that content to an estimated $1.50–$2.00 per handset. The 5G mmWave uplift is larger still: beam-steering switches and phase shifters push RF-SOI content toward $3.00 or above per device — though mmWave penetration beyond the United States and Japan remained limited as of mid-2026. The 2023–2025 supply-chain inventory correction compressed RF-SOI volumes sharply, but by Q2 FY2026 sequential volumes were recovering, up 47 percent versus Q1, signalling that destocking was approaching exhaustion.

## FD-SOI: The Low-Power Frontier

Fully depleted silicon-on-insulator is Soitec's most strategically complex platform and its most deliberate long-cycle bet. The substrate structure is distinctive: the device silicon layer is just 12 nanometres thick — thin enough to deplete fully under gate voltage without doped channel engineering — sitting atop an ultra-thin buried oxide (UTBOX) of roughly 25 nanometres. Below the BOX, the handle silicon serves a second function: a small voltage applied to the back gate shifts the effective threshold voltage of every transistor on the die post-fabrication, enabling dynamic performance-power trade-offs impossible in bulk CMOS or FinFET geometries.

At the 22–28 nm node, FD-SOI delivers 30 to 40 percent lower active power than equivalent bulk CMOS at the same frequency — an advantage that concentrates commercial traction in automotive ADAS processors and MCUs (STMicroelectronics' 28 nm FD-SOI lines at Crolles supply Tier 1 customers including Bosch and Continental) and in low-power IoT and edge-AI inference chips where back-gate tuning enables always-on operation at sub-threshold voltages.

Samsung Foundry entered the ecosystem under a 2014 technology licensing agreement with STMicroelectronics, establishing its 28FDS node at Giheung as a second major production platform. But FD-SOI's foundry optionality remains structurally narrow: beyond ST Crolles and Samsung Giheung, no major foundry had qualified a commercial FD-SOI node as of mid-2026. The contrast with FinFET — available at TSMC, Samsung, Intel Foundry, and GlobalFoundries across multiple nodes — is a genuine competitive constraint on adoption, limiting fabless designers' willingness to commit product roadmaps to a two-source technology.

## POI: The 5G Filter Supercycle

Piezoelectric-on-Insulator is Soitec's fastest-growing platform and the one whose growth mechanics are most immune to the broader mobile inventory correction. The substrate transfers a thin single-crystal film of lithium tantalate (LiTaO₃) or lithium niobate (LiNbO₃) onto a silicon carrier via Smart Cut™. The resulting wafer enables bulk-acoustic-wave filters with steeper roll-off and lower insertion loss than conventional surface-acoustic-wave filters at the mid-band 5G frequencies — the Sub-6 GHz spectrum between 2.5 GHz and 6 GHz where the bulk of global 5G traffic flows.

The filter count escalation from 4G to 5G is the primary demand driver. A 4G LTE smartphone requires approximately 30 to 40 RF filters to manage inter-band interference. A 5G handset — with carrier aggregation across more bands, simultaneous uplink and downlink requirements, and co-existence with 4G, Wi-Fi 6/7, and Bluetooth — requires 70 to 100 filters per device, more than doubling the addressable filter substrate content per phone. Each additional filter is a potential POI wafer consumer, since 5G mid-band performance requirements increasingly exceed what bulk lithium tantalate can deliver without the thermal dissipation and frequency control that a silicon carrier provides.

Qualcomm Technologies formalised this demand signal through a long-term high-volume manufacturing agreement for POI wafers destined for its RF360 front-end module production — the anchor agreement that underwrote Soitec's Singapore capacity expansion. The Pasir Ris Wafer Fab Park facility, whose expansion completed in 2024–2025, doubled annual Singapore production capacity to approximately two million 300 mm-equivalent wafers per year, with significant clean-room allocation directed toward POI lines. MediaTek entered a parallel long-term supply agreement, giving Soitec volume commitments from the two dominant Android RF-chip suppliers simultaneously.

## SmartSiC and the Impairment

Smart Cut's extension to silicon carbide followed a straightforward logic: the cost reduction trajectory for SiC power devices in EV inverters and on-board chargers was constrained partly by expensive bulk SiC substrates, grown by slow physical vapour transport over many days. SmartSiC™ addressed this by transferring a thin SiC epitaxial device layer onto a polycrystalline SiC carrier via ion implantation and bonding, targeting a substrate cost below that of bulk SiC at equivalent device performance — and positioning Soitec to capture value from the electrification supercycle.

By 2024–2025, that arithmetic had collapsed. Chinese SiC substrate manufacturers — including SICC and TianYu, alongside pricing pressure from Coherent's SiC division — compressed global SiC substrate prices well below prior forecasts, eliminating the cost arbitrage SmartSiC required to justify a premium position. In November 2025, Soitec recorded a €41 million impairment of SmartSiC non-current assets in its H1 FY2026 results, the disclosure triggering a 28.7 percent single-day decline in SOI.PA — the sharpest one-day move in the company's recent history.

The impairment did not write off the technology. Soitec's SiC IP and process equipment remain on the balance sheet, and the Smart Cut variant applicable to SiC is demonstrable. But the commercial ramp is effectively paused, and incoming CEO Laurent Rémont — whose background at Infineon spans RF semiconductors and MEMS sensors, not power electronics — faces a decision with limited obvious precedent: persist at reduced capital intensity targeting a SiC premium segment, pivot toward licensing the SmartSiC IP to device manufacturers, or further reduce capital commitments and redeploy toward POI and Photonics-SOI.

## The Remaining Platform Stack

Beyond the four headline platforms, Soitec operates narrower substrate lines that round out a diversified portfolio. RF-GaN — gallium nitride on silicon produced by epitaxial deposition — serves power-amplifier die sets in 5G macro-cell base stations and satellite communications, a market growing modestly with network rollout but small in absolute terms relative to RF-SOI.

Photonics-SOI emerged as the sharpest growth narrative in the non-mobile portfolio through 2025–2026. Silicon-photonics interconnect wafers — SOI substrates engineered for low-loss optical waveguide fabrication — feed the transceiver ASICs that hyperscalers including Google, Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon are deploying in AI compute-cluster interconnects at 400G and 800G. This sub-segment recorded 34 percent organic growth in H1 FY2026, driven by accelerating AI data-centre capital expenditure, even as mobile-facing lines contracted.

Imager-SOI, historically supplied to Sony Semiconductor Solutions for back-illuminated CMOS image sensors, is being phased out as of FY2026 as Sony internalises its substrate supply. Power-SOI serves automotive power management in stable volumes; MEMS-SOI supports microelectromechanical sensor fabrication at specialist IDMs. None individually moves the revenue line, but together they demonstrate the breadth of application to which the ion-implantation and molecular-bonding logic can be extended — the same sequence invented at CEA-Leti in the early 1990s, running unchanged beneath every platform in the portfolio.

chapters.title: Revenue, Margins, and Capital Structure Through the Down-Cycle and Toward the $2 Billion Target
chapters.body:
## The Revenue Arc: From €584 Million to the Billion-Euro Peak and Back

Soitec's financial history across the five fiscal years through March 2025 traces one of the cleanest boom-and-correction arcs in the European semiconductor supply chain. Revenue compounded at roughly 37 percent annually from €583.76 million in FY2021 to €1.09 billion in FY2023 — the fiscal year ended 31 March 2023 — before retracing in two measured steps to €977.91 million in FY2024 and €890.85 million in FY2025. By the first half of FY2026, the trailing-twelve-month run rate had compressed to approximately €784 million, with H1 FY2026 revenue of €231 million alone representing a 29 percent organic decline year-on-year.

The upswing was almost entirely volume-driven. Long-term supply agreements — typically three-to-five year contracts priced per wafer — mean Soitec's revenue follows foundry wafer-start schedules rather than spot-price movements. The FY2021–FY2023 surge reflected two simultaneous forces: the 5G handset supercycle pulling through GlobalFoundries' RF-SOI output at Fab 9 in Malta, New York, and the TSMC and UMC RF-SOI lines in Taiwan; and early POI (piezoelectric-on-insulator) revenues beginning to appear as Qualcomm's RF360 front-end module programme moved from qualification toward volume production in Singapore. FD-SOI, supplied primarily to STMicroelectronics at Crolles, contributed steady growth as automotive MCU and IoT designs on ST's 28 nm FD-SOI node accumulated design wins. Together, RF-SOI accounted for the majority of the €506 million in cumulative revenue added between FY2021 and FY2023, with POI providing a structurally new and growing increment and FD-SOI a durable base.

The correction that followed was the mirror image. Mobile handset sell-through decelerated across 2023 and into 2024, prompting the RF front-end module supply chain — Qorvo, Skyworks, Murata, Qualcomm RF360 — to draw down accumulated inventory rather than place new substrate orders. Soitec's foundry customers responded by reducing wafer-start schedules, translating directly into lower SOI wafer pull. The FY2024 revenue decline of 10.2 percent and the FY2025 decline of 8.9 percent were not price concessions; they were volume concessions on contracts whose per-wafer economics remained stable. The Automotive & Industrial segment compounded the decline: SmartSiC commercial ramp stalled ahead of the H1 FY2026 impairment, and the broader automotive semiconductor inventory correction suppressed FD-SOI orders from STMicroelectronics' automotive customer base. By H1 FY2026, Automotive & Industrial had fallen 74 percent year-on-year to just €15 million — barely 6 percent of the revenue mix — against a peak contribution that had represented the strategic growth pillar of the €2 billion ambition.

The concentration of revenue among three foundry relationships — GlobalFoundries for RF-SOI, STMicroelectronics for FD-SOI, and TSMC and UMC collectively for RF-SOI and emerging POI — is the structural vulnerability embedded in this model. While Soitec does not disclose customer-specific revenue shares, the product-line logic implies that any two of the three principal relationships together likely account for the majority of billings. The corollary of that concentration is the pricing stability those relationships afford: a foundry that has spent 12 to 24 months qualifying a substrate node does not switch suppliers over a wafer-price renegotiation, leaving Soitec's per-wafer economics largely insulated from the volume correction.

## Margin Architecture Through the Trough

The more instructive financial story of the down-cycle is not the revenue decline but the EBITDA margin floor. [Soitec FY2025 results](https://www.soitec.com/docs/default-source/financial-reports/2024-2025/en/soitec-fy25-results-presentation.pdf) showed an EBITDA margin of 33.5 percent on €890.85 million of revenue, implying an EBITDA of approximately €298 million. At the FY2023 peak, with volumes running roughly 22 percent higher, the EBITDA margin was likely in the 35–36 percent range — consistent with the operating leverage of an asset-heavy process company running near full capacity. The implied EBITDA contraction from peak to FY2025 trough, therefore, was approximately €85–95 million on a revenue decline of roughly €199 million: EBITDA fell at less than half the rate of revenue, compressing the margin by only 200–250 basis points.

| Period | Revenue (€M) | Est. EBITDA (€M) | EBITDA Margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2023 (peak) | 1,090 | ~392 | ~36% |
| FY2024 | 978 | ~332 | ~34% |
| FY2025 | 891 | ~298 | 33.5% |
| H1 FY2026 | 231 | 79 | 34.1% |

Comparable specialty materials peers — Entegris, CMC Materials, and the commodity silicon wafer producers at the lower-margin end — typically absorb 500 to 800 basis points of EBITDA margin compression when volumes fall 15 to 20 percent, as fixed-cost absorption spreads across fewer units while raw material and energy costs remain sticky. Soitec's 200–250 basis-point resilience reflects three structural factors: first, the long-term supply agreements lock in a degree of volume commitment that limits the worst-case downside; second, the Bernin campus fixed-cost base, once built, does not scale linearly with volume — R&D and process-engineering headcount carry on regardless of wafer throughput; and third, the per-wafer pricing in existing contracts does not reset to spot at volume reductions, preserving revenue per unit shipped. H1 FY2026's 34.1 percent EBITDA margin — actually slightly above FY2025's full-year rate — demonstrates that the business retains its earnings architecture even at severely depressed volumes.

## The H1 FY2026 P&L: Dissecting the Net Loss

The €67 million net loss reported in [H1 FY2026](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/11/19/3191252/0/en/SOITEC-SOITEC-REPORTS-SECOND-QUARTER-REVENUE-AND-HALF-YEAR-RESULTS-OF-FISCAL-YEAR-2026.html) requires decomposition before it can be read as a signal of operational distress — which it is not. The P&L below the €79 million EBITDA line was dominated by three non-recurring or non-cash items that obscured a business that remained marginally profitable on its underlying operations.

The €41 million SmartSiC impairment was a write-down of non-current assets — not a cash outflow — following a strategic reassessment of the silicon carbide market prompted by accelerating Chinese entrant pricing pressure. The €19 million foreign-exchange loss reflected the euro's appreciation against the US dollar across the six months to September 2025, compressing the euro value of dollar-denominated revenues (RF-SOI and POI contracts are typically dollar-invoiced to foundry customers in the United States, Taiwan, and Singapore). The €3 million Dolphin Design depreciation related to Soitec's embedded-software subsidiary, a legacy holding that contributes modest revenues but carries amortisable acquired intangibles. Strip those three items from the P&L and the adjusted current net result was approximately negative €2 million — the operational business held essentially to breakeven at the revenue trough, a feat that most specialty semiconductor material suppliers would struggle to replicate.

## Capital Structure: Conservative by Design

Soitec's balance sheet as of the most recent reporting dates reflects a management team that funded the Singapore expansion without leveraging the company into vulnerability. Shareholders' equity stood at €1.6 billion as of 31 March 2025, having grown approximately €100 million year-on-year. Gross financial debt rose from €782 million in March 2025 to €953 million in September 2025 as construction drawdowns for the Pasir Ris Wafer Fab Park expansion reached their closing tranches. Against €808 million of cash held at 30 September 2025, net financial debt was €145 million — a net debt-to-LTM-EBITDA ratio of approximately 0.5 times.

That leverage ratio stands in sharp contrast to the 2.0x–3.0x net debt-to-EBITDA common among capital-intensive semiconductor peers investing through cycles. The practical implication is that Soitec can sustain its approximately €140 million FY2026 capex programme, its R&D budget (historically in the range of 10–12 percent of revenue), and its Singapore commissioning costs entirely from operating cash flow and existing cash reserves without accessing equity markets or straining debt covenants. The conservative balance sheet is simultaneously a competitive advantage — allowing continued investment in POI process maturation and Photonics-SOI qualification while competitors retrench — and a legitimate question from capital-markets participants who observed the stock trading at roughly €25 per share in late 2025, down approximately 75 percent from its 2022 peak near €350, asking why the company had not repurchased shares at a trough valuation below book equity.

## The Path to $2 Billion: Decomposing the Growth Requirement

The medium-term revenue target of $2 billion (approximately €1.85 billion at 2026 exchange rates) with 40 percent EBITDA margin is an ambitious but internally consistent ambition, provided three growth vectors materialise on schedule.

RF-SOI and POI together — the Mobile Communications segment — must recover and grow from the H1 FY2026 trough of €119 million per half to a substantially higher run rate as 5G handset volumes stabilise and the mix shift toward 5G mmWave and early 6G architectures increases the substrate-content-per-phone. POI in particular represents structurally new addressable revenue: each 5G mmWave RF front-end module requires more complex bulk-acoustic-wave and surface-acoustic-wave filters than its Sub-6 GHz predecessor, and Soitec's Qualcomm and MediaTek supply agreements underwrite volume growth as those filter designs reach production scale in Singapore.

Edge & Cloud AI, which expanded 34 percent organically in H1 FY2026 even as the total company contracted, represents the structural offset and upside optionality. Photonics-SOI wafers for hyperscaler optical transceiver ASICs are growing faster than any other platform and carry comparable margins; FD-SOI automotive and industrial design wins at STMicroelectronics continue to accumulate as 22 nm FD-SOI becomes the standard node for ADAS processors.

| Scenario | FY2026 Base (€M) | Target (€M) | Required Years | Implied CAGR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5-year recovery | ~600 | ~1,850 | 5 | ~25% |
| 4-year recovery | ~600 | ~1,850 | 4 | ~32% |
| Historical FY21–FY23 reference | — | — | 2 | ~37% |

A 25 percent CAGR over five years is demanding but historically plausible: the FY2021–FY2023 growth phase averaged 37 percent annually on a larger base. The 40 percent EBITDA margin target is achievable at higher volumes because the Bernin and Singapore fixed-cost structures are largely installed, meaning incremental revenue above the current trough will absorb overhead at a lower per-wafer rate and lift margins toward — and potentially above — the historical peak.

## Capex Normalisation and the Next Build Decision

FY2026 capex guidance of approximately €140 million marks the decisive step down from the Singapore-build peak of an estimated €250–300 million across FY2023–FY2025. That normalisation has two effects: it restores free cash flow to positive territory (FY2025 already turned to positive €26 million after the negative €43 million in FY2024), and it redirects management attention from construction project execution back to process R&D and customer engagement.

Whether €140 million per year is sufficient to support the volume targets through FY2030 depends on how quickly POI and Photonics-SOI volumes scale. Singapore's newly doubled capacity of approximately two million 300 mm-equivalent wafers per year provides meaningful headroom for the near-term recovery. Should POI demand from Qualcomm and MediaTek accelerate ahead of expectations — or should Photonics-SOI demand from hyperscaler AI interconnect programmes prove larger than the base case — a new capacity commitment could be required in FY2027 or FY2028. That would mean returning to a capital-expenditure envelope of €200 million or more, resetting the free-cash-flow profile and requiring Soitec either to draw further on its €808 million cash reserve or to tap debt markets at what would then be lower leverage. New CEO Laurent Rémont inherits a balance sheet capable of funding that decision. Whether the strategic logic — particularly for SmartSiC versus a narrower focus on RF-SOI, POI, and Photonics-SOI — justifies the commitment is the question that will define the capital allocation narrative of his tenure.

chapters.title: Quarter by Quarter: Management Commentary, Guidance Cadence, and the Mobile Recovery
chapters.body:
## The Revenue Arc: From Peak to Trough

The quarterly revenue strip that emerged from Soitec's reporting cycle between April 2024 and February 2026 told a story of compressed inventory, a stubborn mobile correction, and the tentative first signs of a volume inflection. At [€890.85 million](https://www.soitec.com/docs/default-source/financial-reports/2024-2025/en/soitec-fy25-results-presentation.pdf) for the fiscal year ended 31 March 2025 — a second consecutive annual decline, following the 10.2 percent drop in FY2024 from the FY2023 peak of €1.09 billion — the company had spent two years absorbing the consequences of a 5G smartphone supercycle that had collapsed into inventory normalisation. What the headline annual number obscured was the sharpness of the quarterly deceleration that continued well into the new fiscal year.

| Quarter | Revenue | Sequential Change | Year-on-Year |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 FY2025 (Apr–Jun 2024) | ~€224M | — | — |
| Q2 FY2025 (Jul–Sep 2024) | ~€222M | ~−1% | — |
| FY2025 Full Year | €890.85M | — | −8.9% |
| Q1 FY2026 (Apr–Jun 2025) | ~€92M (implied) | ~−59% | ~−59% |
| Q2 FY2026 (Jul–Sep 2025) | [€139M](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/11/19/3191252/0/en/SOITEC-SOITEC-REPORTS-SECOND-QUARTER-REVENUE-AND-HALF-YEAR-RESULTS-OF-FISCAL-YEAR-2026.html) | +47% | ~−37% |
| Q3 FY2026 (Oct–Dec 2025) | Guided: ~€146–152M | +5% to +9% organic | — |

The pivot came in Q2 FY2026, when revenue reached €139 million — a 47 percent sequential rebound from the €92 million posted in Q1. Even accounting for seasonal patterns that have historically made Soitec's September quarter stronger than its June quarter, the magnitude of that swing signalled that RF-SOI volume withheld during the RF front-end inventory correction was beginning to flow again through GlobalFoundries' Malta fab and the Taiwan foundry lines. The aggregate H1 FY2026 result of €231 million — a 29 percent organic decline year-on-year from the comparable period — confirmed the trough was Q1 FY2026, and that Q2 represented, at minimum, a floor.

## Pierre Barnabé's Final Half: Commentary Under Pressure

When outgoing chief executive Pierre Barnabé presented the [H1 FY2026 results](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/11/19/3191252/0/en/SOITEC-SOITEC-REPORTS-SECOND-QUARTER-REVENUE-AND-HALF-YEAR-RESULTS-OF-FISCAL-YEAR-2026.html) in November 2025, his characterisation of the period captured both the cyclical and structural dimensions of the performance:

> "Q2 FY2026 performance reflected strong Edge & Cloud AI momentum offset by Mobile inventory correction and weak Automotive."

The framing was deliberate. Barnabé did not describe the mobile correction as resolved; instead he positioned Q2 as sequential recovery within an ongoing normalisation. On the POI ramp, he pointed to volume uptake through Qualcomm's RF360 front-end module supply chain as a key driver of sequential mobile improvement, though precise volume commitments under the long-term supply agreement remained commercially sensitive. For Q3, management guided to "mid-to-high single-digit sequential growth organic" from the €139 million Q2 base — language that implied cautious optimism without committing to the pace of recovery investors had been hoping for since the correction began in late 2022.

## The Structural Story in the Mix

The H1 FY2026 segment breakdown was the most analytically significant element of the results package, revealing a business whose revenue composition had shifted materially from its pre-cycle profile.

| Segment | H1 FY2026 | YoY Change | Mix Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mobile Communications | €119M | −30% | ~52% |
| Automotive & Industrial | €15M | −74% | ~6% |
| Edge & Cloud AI | €96M | +34% (ex-Imager-SOI) | ~42% |

Mobile Communications — spanning RF-SOI for GlobalFoundries, TSMC, and UMC, together with POI for Qualcomm's filter module supply chain — contracted 30 percent year-on-year to €119 million. The decline was volume-driven: wafer pricing under long-term supply agreements is sticky by design, meaning the drop reflected curtailed foundry pull-orders as handset OEM supply chains worked down the RF front-end inventory accumulated during the 2022 supercycle build.

The collapse in Automotive & Industrial, down 74 percent year-on-year to just €15 million, had two components. The first was the SmartSiC pause, which effectively froze commercial volume shipments into EV power-electronics applications pending the strategic review of the programme. The second was the broader automotive semiconductor inventory correction, which caused STMicroelectronics and other FD-SOI foundry customers to reduce wafer starts across automotive MCU and power management product lines throughout 2024–2025.

Against that backdrop, the 34 percent organic growth in Edge & Cloud AI — to €96 million, representing approximately 42 percent of H1 FY2026 revenue versus roughly 35 percent in the comparable prior-year period — carried structural significance extending beyond the immediate cycle. Photonics-SOI wafers consumed in silicon-photonics optical transceiver ASICs for AI compute-cluster interconnects, and FD-SOI substrates for edge AI inference SoCs, were both growing off expanding contractual volumes. The arithmetic carried an implication Barnabé did not need to state explicitly: Soitec entering the mobile recovery with Edge & Cloud AI at 42 percent of revenue is materially less handset-cycle-sensitive than the company of FY2023, when mobile represented approximately 55 percent of the mix. Each percentage point shift in segment mix toward Edge & Cloud AI reduces the amplitude of the next RF front-end inventory correction.

## The SmartSiC Shock

The H1 FY2026 results were accompanied by the most consequential single disclosure of the Barnabé era. On 20 November 2025, alongside the half-year financials, Soitec announced a €41 million impairment of SmartSiC non-current assets — reflecting a downward revision to silicon carbide substrate market prospects driven by accelerating pricing pressure from Chinese SiC entrants. The market reaction was categorical: the stock fell 28.7 percent in a single session, from €34.67 to €24.73, erasing more than €600 million of market capitalisation and bringing shares to levels last seen before the height of the 5G buildout.

The impairment crystallised a competitive dynamic that sell-side analysts had been tracking with increasing concern through 2024 but had not fully priced. The majority of models covering SOI.PA had assumed Soitec could defend a premium positioning for its bonded Smart Cut variant of SiC substrates — a thesis the company had actively supported with references to differentiated technology advantages over conventional SiC boule-grown wafers. The €41 million charge invalidated that assumption in a single filing. In the days following, several brokers reduced price targets sharply; pre-impairment consensus estimates for FY2026 full-year revenue, which had stood at approximately €822 million, were withdrawn or revised downward as analysts restructured their models around a SmartSiC pause of indeterminate duration. Short interest in SOI.PA rose in the weeks that followed as the strategic review — and the question of what incoming CEO Laurent Rémont would decide to do with the programme — remained unresolved.

## Q3 Guidance and the Recovery Calculus

The February 2026 Q3 revenue announcement gave investors the next data point in the recovery sequence. Management guided for "mid-to-high single-digit sequential growth organic" from the Q2 €139 million base. Translated into a revenue range:

- **Mid single-digit (+5%):** approximately €146 million
- **High single-digit (+9%):** approximately €152 million

Summing H1 FY2026 at €231 million, a Q3 at approximately €146–152 million, and an assumed Q4 with further sequential improvement toward €160–175 million yields a full-year FY2026 outturn of approximately €580–620 million — consistent with guidance signals embedded in the H1 results presentation. Against the pre-impairment consensus of approximately €822 million, the implied full-year figure represented a shortfall of 25–30 percent. It also represented, on the recovery thesis, the year containing the trough: Q1 FY2026 at €92 million would, if the sequential trajectory held, prove to be the cyclical nadir.

## Disclosure Cadence and the Visibility Gap

Soitec's investor communication framework — quarterly revenue-only press releases in approximately August, November, February, and May, with half-year P&L disclosures in November and May — provides more reporting touchpoints than many mid-cap European industrials but fewer data dimensions per release than the quarterly full P&L standard in the United States. For a company with Soitec's financial architecture, the format creates a specific analytical problem.

Because revenue is the critical input into any earnings power model for a high-fixed-cost specialty substrate business, the quarterly revenue announcement is the most predictive single filing. But it carries no segment breakdown: that information appears only at the biannual P&L disclosure. Investors following the recovery in Q3 FY2026 knew the aggregate sequential growth figure but could not distinguish from public data alone whether POI was ramping ahead of RF-SOI, or whether Edge & Cloud AI momentum was accelerating or beginning to plateau. For a company whose investment thesis was increasingly organised around the claim that structural exposure to AI workloads was improving its through-cycle earnings quality, the absence of quarterly segment colour represented a meaningful gap in the information set — one that the new leadership team under Laurent Rémont would eventually need to address if it wished to compress the discount that uncertainty was extracting from the share price.

chapters.title: The Rémont Era Begins: CEO Transition, Executive Team Cohesion, and Board Architecture
chapters.body:
## A Successor Forged in the Same Ecosystem

When Soitec's board of directors gathered in January 2026 to ratify its choice of chief executive, the decision carried a logic that bordered on the biographical. Laurent Rémont, fifty-four years old and freshly departed from Infineon Technologies, had spent his professional life circling the exact problems Soitec now needed him to solve. His engineering degree from Grenoble INP–ENSERG planted him squarely in the Isère semiconductor corridor — the same stretch of the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes where Soitec was founded, where CEA-Leti incubated Smart Cut™, and where STMicroelectronics operates the Crolles fab that remains Soitec's largest FD-SOI foundry customer. Geography, in this industry, is not incidental: Isère's concentration of substrate physicists, process engineers, and RF design teams is a talent ecosystem, and Rémont's formation within it gave him a tacit fluency that no number of consultancy briefings could replicate.

His career path thereafter reads as a methodical tour of the technologies Soitec now bets its future on. More than fifteen years at STMicroelectronics — spanning general management and R&D roles across Europe and Asia — put him in proximity to FD-SOI process development at a time when the technology was being co-engineered between ST's Crolles facility, CEA-Leti, and Soitec's wafer supply lines. He then moved to Kontron AG as chief technology officer, acquiring embedded-computing perspective on the industrial and automotive end-markets that Soitec's FD-SOI and SmartSiC platforms are targeting. The most directly relevant chapter came at Infineon Technologies, where as Senior Vice President heading the Radio Frequency and Sensors division he oversaw a business encompassing MEMS microphones, pressure sensors, and RF switch products — substrate-intensive, filter-adjacent, architecturally close to the POI and RF-SOI products that constitute the bulk of Soitec's mobile revenue. Rémont joined Soitec on 16 March 2026 as a special adviser to his predecessor, formally assuming the chief executive role on 1 April 2026, subject to ratification as a board director at the Annual General Meeting expected in July 2026. [GlobeNewswire, January 2026](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/01/08/3215061/0/en/SOITEC-BOARD-OF-DIRECTORS-APPOINTS-LAURENT-R%C3%89MONT-CHIEF-EXECUTIVE-OFFICER-EFFECTIVE-APRIL-2026.html)

## The Barnabé Inheritance: Scale, Singapore, and a Contested Bet

To understand what Rémont inherited, one must fairly assess the nine years of Pierre Barnabé. When Barnabé assumed the chief executive role in 2017, Soitec was completing its exit from a costly diversification experiment — solar energy and LED substrates had nearly destroyed the company in the early 2010s — and was refocusing entirely on its core SOI and engineered substrate franchises. What he built over the following six years was a disciplined scaling operation: revenue roughly doubled from approximately €600 million toward the FY2023 peak of €1.09 billion, driven by the structural upgrade of the global smartphone fleet from 4G to 5G and the corresponding explosion in RF front-end module complexity. His signature capital allocation call — the decision to expand the Singapore Pasir Ris Wafer Fab Park, a construction programme that began in December 2022 and was completed in 2024–2025 — more than doubled the site's annual capacity to approximately two million 300mm-equivalent wafers per year, underwriting long-term volume agreements with Qualcomm and MediaTek and cementing Singapore as the volume manufacturing anchor for the POI commercial ramp.

Barnabé announced his resignation on 1 October 2025, effective 31 March 2026. The timing proved awkward. Approximately six weeks later, in November 2025, Soitec disclosed a €41 million impairment charge against SmartSiC non-current assets, triggering a 28.7 percent single-day share price collapse. The sequence raises a question that will follow Barnabé's legacy for years: was the SmartSiC program a strategic mistake, or sound thesis executed into a market that moved too slowly? The honest answer is probably both. The structural logic — using a Smart Cut variant to produce thinner, more efficient SiC substrates for EV power electronics — was technologically credible and commercially ambitious. The error was the pace of the capital commitment relative to the rate at which Chinese SiC entrants compressed pricing in 2024–2025, faster than any bull-case scenario had anticipated. Whether the board's recruitment of Frédéric Lissalde (former BorgWarner CEO, automotive electrification background) as Chairman in March 2025 was intended partly to accelerate SmartSiC commercial traction through his automotive OEM network, and whether the impairment nine months later represents a repudiation of that thesis, is a question the company has not addressed directly in public communications.

## The Executive Committee: Continuity Anchors and New Commercial Blood

The executive team Rémont leads is a deliberate hybrid of institutional memory and recently recruited commercial capability. At one extreme sits Christophe Maleville, Chief Technology Officer since 1993 — one year after the company's founding — whose thirty-plus years of Smart Cut™ process development, approximately thirty patents, and doctorate in microelectronics from Grenoble supplemented by an INSEAD MBA constitute a depth of substrate IP governance that is effectively irreplaceable. Maleville's continuity across this CEO transition is a material source of stability: he knows where every process secret lives, which customer qualification histories matter, and which of the company's eighteen annual patent filings are genuinely defensive versus exploratory. Alongside him, Chief Operating Officer Cyril Menon, in post since 2006 with an IBM semiconductor background and Harvard management training, provides the operational discipline that sustains above-30-percent EBITDA margins through a revenue trough.

Against these long-tenured anchors, four of the nine executive committee members joined between 2023 and 2026, reshaping the commercial and financial leadership profile substantially. Albin Jacquemont (CFO since May 2025, previously Group CFO at Inetum, SAUR, Altran, and Darty plc) brings a services and infrastructure finance background that differs markedly from Soitec's capital-intensive semiconductor context — a gap the board presumably judged acceptable given the quality of the underlying financial controls already in place. René Jonker (Chief Product Officer since October 2025, formerly of ams AG, NXP, and Nexperia) brings a product strategy perspective shaped by the same analog semiconductor and sensor supply chains that feed into Soitec's substrate customer base. Calvin Chen, acting Chief Sales Officer since December 2025 and a Soitec employee since 2010, holds a Stanford economics degree and is Singapore-based — a useful profile given that Asia Pacific accounts for the majority of Soitec's foundry customer interactions. The key question for the $2 billion revenue ambition is whether this group of newer executives, whose substrate-domain knowledge is necessarily shallower than Maleville's and Menon's, can absorb enough technical context to close the commercial cycles that define engineered-wafer revenue growth.

## Board Architecture: French Sovereignty and Independent Oversight

Soitec's twelve-member board carries an unusual dual character: rigorously independent on most conventional governance metrics, yet anchored by two French state-linked institutions whose combined ownership creates a de facto sovereignty layer over strategic decisions. [Soitec Board of Directors](https://www.soitec.com/home/investors/governance/board-of-directors)

The state anchor positions are held by Samuel Dalens (Bpifrance Participations, 11.49% shareholder, École Polytechnique and Télécom Paris) and Julie Galland (CEA Investissement, 7.21% shareholder, Director of Technological Research at CEA, PhD solid-state physics from École Polytechnique). Their combined ~18.7% stake and board seats give the French state an influence over major strategic decisions — including M&A, technology licensing, and capital allocation — that would be unrecognisable in the governance structure of a US-listed peer with a dispersed institutional register. The argument that this structure has protected French technology sovereignty is supported by the observable facts: Smart Cut™ IP has remained domiciled in France through thirty years of commercial expansion; the original CEA-Leti licensing agreements have not been restructured in ways that would dilute the state's position; and no acquirer has successfully dislodged the anchor ownership bloc. The cost is strategic flexibility. Any transaction or licensing decision that a purely institutional shareholder register might approve on financial merit alone must be stress-tested against the sovereignty calculus of the French public investment bank and the nuclear and research agency whose original scientists invented the core technology.

The board's other notable feature is the presence of Satoshi Onishi, former President and CEO of Shin-Etsu Handotai Europe, as a non-independent director representing the historical SEH relationship. This cross-directorship reflects the 1997 cross-licensing agreement that gave SEH access to Smart Cut™ and validated Soitec's IP commercially. SEH is simultaneously a licensee producing commodity SOI wafers using Smart Cut™ variants and, at the lower end of the market, a potential competitor. The conflict-of-interest management protocols around that directorship are not disclosed in detail in public governance documents, but the structure is acknowledged in Soitec's board composition disclosures. Françoise Chombar, co-founder of Melexis, provides independent semiconductor industry perspective from a position unconstrained by any customer or supplier relationship. Chairman Frédéric Lissalde (Engineering ENSAM, MBA HEC) rounds out the board's profile with automotive powertrain and electrification credentials relevant to the SmartSiC thesis, even as that thesis is being reassessed.

The board is 60 percent women (excluding employee directors) and 70 percent independent, with an average age of 53 — figures that represent meaningful progress for a French industrial company in a capital-goods sector where board diversity has historically lagged.

## Incentives and the $2 Billion Alignment Signal

The AGM proxy materials published ahead of the July 2026 meeting were expected to detail the performance share plan attached to Rémont's appointment, including any conditions linked to revenue thresholds, EBITDA margins, or stock price recovery. As of the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, the specific performance conditions had not yet been publicly disclosed in final form pending AGM ratification of his directorship. The $2 billion revenue ambition — articulated under Barnabé and not yet formally restated by Rémont — implies roughly an 80 percent increase from the approximately €1.1 billion FY2025 base. Any long-term incentive plan tying significant equity vesting to that target would constitute a meaningful alignment signal for outside investors; its absence or dilution, conversely, would prompt questions about whether the board has quietly lowered its own expectations.

What is clear from the public record is that Rémont accepted a role in the middle of a documented crisis — a 20-percent revenue decline from peak, a €41 million impairment in a program his predecessor had staked reputational capital on, and a share price near multi-year lows. His CV suggests he was chosen not to maintain a steady state but to reset commercial strategy around the substrate platforms — RF-SOI, POI, FD-SOI — where his Infineon RF and sensor background provides the most direct customer-facing credibility. Whether the Maleville-Menon operational spine can sustain margin discipline while Rémont rebuilds the growth narrative is the governance bet the board made on 8 January 2026.

chapters.title: The Foundry Ecosystem: GlobalFoundries, STMicro, TSMC, Qualcomm, and the 5G Value Chain
chapters.body:
## The Indirect Model and Why It Matters

Soitec does not sell chips. It sells the ground beneath them — engineered substrates that foundries and integrated device manufacturers transform, through months of photolithography and ion implantation, into the radio-frequency switches, filters, and edge-AI processors that eventually reach consumers inside an iPhone or a Tesla. That one layer of intermediation, structural rather than accidental, shapes almost every dimension of the company's commercial risk profile.

The supply chain runs in two distinct tiers. In the first, Soitec contracts with foundries and IDMs — GlobalFoundries, STMicroelectronics, TSMC, UMC, and Samsung Foundry — under long-term volume agreements that typically span three to five years, priced per wafer in euros. These customers take physical delivery of the substrates, run their own proprietary process flows on top, and sell finished die to fabless companies and module makers. In the second tier, those fabless players — Qualcomm, MediaTek, Apple's supply chain, Murata, Skyworks, Qorvo — sell RF front-end modules or SoCs into OEM supply chains that ultimately determine smartphone and automobile production volumes. Soitec is exposed to that end-market demand, but insulated from OEM concentration risk: no single handset brand or car manufacturer directly negotiates with Bernin. The counterparty is always the foundry.

That insulation, however, is symmetrical. When foundry utilisation rates collapse — as they did in 2023–2025 when the RF front-end inventory correction swept through GlobalFoundries and TSMC's RF lines — Soitec's wafer shipment volumes fall in lockstep with foundry loading, regardless of what Apple's retail sell-through looks like. Revenue peaked at €1.09 billion in fiscal year 2023 and contracted to €890.85 million by fiscal year 2025, a two-year decline of roughly 18 percent, driven almost entirely by foundry underloading rather than any loss of design wins or customer relationships. The structural exposure is to utilisation, not to brand concentration.

## GlobalFoundries: The RF-SOI Anchor

GlobalFoundries occupies a position in the Soitec revenue model that is, without serious exaggeration, irreplaceable at any near-term horizon. GF's Fab 9 in Malta, New York, is the world's dominant production site for RF switch and low-noise-amplifier silicon, running the [45RFSOI platform](https://www.globalfoundries.com/technology-solutions/rf) — a 45 nm silicon-on-insulator node purpose-engineered for high-frequency, low-loss radio-frequency circuits. Every RF front-end module in a mass-market smartphone that routes antenna signals across 4G, 5G Sub-6 GHz, and Wi-Fi 6 bands almost certainly contains GF 45RFSOI die; the customer list at that node reads like a register of the RF semiconductor industry — Qualcomm's RF360 business, Apple's supply chain partners, Murata, and Skyworks all depend on Malta.

Soitec supplies the high-resistivity RF-SOI wafers on which GF runs those process flows. The relationship deepened further when Soitec announced an agreement to supply wafers to GF's newer 9SW platform, also at Fab 9, which targets next-generation 5G and Wi-Fi 7 chip production at improved frequency performance and lower insertion loss than 45RFSOI. The 9SW engagement is strategically significant beyond its near-term volume: it extends Soitec's designed-in position at GF into the next technology node transition, ensuring that the substrate supplier relationship is refreshed rather than grandfathered when foundry customers migrate their most advanced RF flows.

GF's RF business, which the company began separately disclosing after its 2021 NYSE IPO, provides the clearest available proxy for Soitec's RF-SOI wafer demand. When GF reports RF revenue pressure — as it did through calendar 2023 and 2024 — Soitec's RF wafer shipment volumes compress accordingly. The recovery visible in Soitec's Q2 FY2026 data (+47 percent sequentially versus Q1) was broadly consistent with GF's own commentary on RF utilisation normalisation as the handset channel inventory correction unwound.

## STMicroelectronics: Collaborative Customer, Vulnerable Anchor

The STMicroelectronics relationship is categorically different from the GlobalFoundries dynamic. ST is not merely a customer — it is a co-architect. The 28 nm and 22 nm FD-SOI process nodes running at ST's Crolles fab in the Isère valley, a short drive from Soitec's Bernin campus, emerged from a tripartite collaboration between ST, CEA-Leti, and Soitec that stretches back to the early 2010s. The STM32 automotive microcontroller family, ST's IoT SoCs, and its power management integrated circuits — products generating billions in annual revenue for ST — are manufactured on Soitec's ultra-thin buried-oxide FD-SOI substrates, where the back-gate biasing architecture provides 30 to 40 percent lower dynamic power than equivalent bulk CMOS processes at comparable lithography nodes.

That collaborative depth cuts both ways. It makes substitution effectively impossible: Crolles' process qualification is built around Soitec's specific BOX thickness specifications and doping profiles, and re-qualifying an alternative substrate would require 12 to 24 months of destructive testing. But it also means that when ST's own business deteriorates, Soitec's FD-SOI wafer volumes deteriorate with it without the buffer of a competitive re-sourcing threat.

The near-term risk is real. STMicroelectronics announced a substantial restructuring in early 2025, including headcount reductions and capacity adjustments at Crolles, reflecting a demand slowdown in the automotive microcontroller market and a broader correction in industrial semiconductor inventories. Crolles capacity utilisation, which had run at elevated levels through the 2021–2023 demand surge, came off sharply — contributing to the 74 percent year-on-year decline in Soitec's Automotive & Industrial segment revenue in H1 FY2026, which fell to €15 million. The structural thesis for FD-SOI in automotive ADAS and edge AI inference remains intact; the near-term volume trajectory is hostage to ST's own recovery timeline and the pace of Crolles utilisation normalisation.

## Qualcomm, MediaTek, and the POI Singapore Bet

If the RF-SOI book represents Soitec's largest single revenue line, the POI programme represents its most consequential strategic investment. Piezoelectric-on-Insulator wafers — which transfer a single-crystal lithium tantalate or lithium niobate film onto a silicon carrier via a Smart Cut variant — are the substrate input for bulk-acoustic-wave filters in 5G RF front-end modules. As handsets migrated from 4G to 5G and began incorporating mmWave bands, the filter count per phone increased sharply, and the performance requirements for those filters demanded POI-based BAW architectures that older aluminium-nitride-on-silicon processes could not meet.

Soitec secured a long-term high-volume manufacturing agreement with Qualcomm Technologies for POI supply destined for Qualcomm RF360 front-end module production — an agreement that effectively underwrote the business case for the Singapore capacity expansion. Construction at the Pasir Ris Wafer Fab Park broke ground in December 2022; the facility completed commissioning in 2024–2025, approximately doubling Singapore's annual production capacity to roughly two million 300 mm-equivalent wafers per year. MediaTek signed a parallel POI supply agreement, providing a second anchor customer for the same capacity and reducing single-customer concentration risk on the Singapore investment.

The Singapore build required substantial capital — gross financial debt rose from €782 million at March 2025 to €953 million at September 2025 as construction drawdowns peaked — but the long-term supply agreements with Qualcomm and MediaTek provide the volume visibility that justifies the commitment. As 5G handset penetration continues in emerging markets and as mmWave deployments expand in North America and Japan, the substrate-content-per-phone on POI filters expands structurally, independent of flat aggregate unit volumes.

## Samsung, Ecosystem Leverage, and the 28FDS Question

Samsung Foundry's 28FDS node represents the third vector through which FD-SOI substrate demand could scale. Under a 2014 licensing agreement with STMicroelectronics, Samsung gained access to FD-SOI process technology and deployed it at its Giheung fab, positioning the node commercially as an alternative to bulk CMOS 28 nm for fabless designers seeking the back-gate power advantage. Samsung is both an indirect substrate customer and a potential ecosystem multiplier: its packaging capabilities and advanced node adjacency could attract fabless AI chip designers — particularly those building automotive inference accelerators — to adopt FD-SOI more broadly than the ST-anchored ecosystem alone would generate.

The commercial performance of 28FDS has, however, been modest relative to early aspirations. Samsung's strategic priority through 2023–2025 was its 4 nm and 3 nm gate-all-around nodes, which consumed the bulk of its foundry marketing investment and customer engagement. The 28FDS node has not generated the design-win velocity that would have converted it from a niche offering into a major pull on Soitec's FD-SOI wafer volumes. Whether new CEO Laurent Rémont — who brings STMicroelectronics heritage and direct FD-SOI familiarity to Bernin — can reinvigorate that ecosystem push is one of the more tractable strategic levers available to him.

## Silicon Photonics and the Hyperscaler Pull

The fastest-growing segment in Soitec's portfolio during the current down-cycle has been, paradoxically, one of its least-discussed platforms. Photonics-SOI — silicon-on-insulator wafers optimised for low-loss optical waveguide fabrication — grew 34 percent organically in H1 FY2026, pulling the Edge & Cloud AI segment to €96 million (42 percent of group revenue) even as Mobile and Automotive contracted sharply.

The demand driver is unambiguous: hyperscalers accelerating AI compute cluster buildouts at 400G and 800G interconnect speeds require optical transceiver ASICs in enormous volumes, and those ASICs are fabricated on silicon photonics wafers that Soitec supplies into the foundry ecosystem. The precise end-customer identities remain opaque in Soitec's public disclosures — the company identifies the segment but does not name the hyperscaler programmes it feeds — but the capital expenditure commitments disclosed by Google, Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon for AI infrastructure in calendar years 2025 and 2026 provide the macro backdrop. Tower Semiconductor and IMEC operate silicon photonics process platforms that are plausible candidates within Soitec's photonics customer base; TSMC's SiPho process flow, which supports co-packaged optics programmes for custom AI accelerator development, represents another likely channel.

| Segment | H1 FY2026 Revenue | YoY Change | Share of Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mobile Communications | €119 million | −30% | 52% |
| Automotive & Industrial | €15 million | −74% | 6% |
| Edge & Cloud AI | €96 million | +34% (organic) | 42% |
| **Total** | **€231 million** | **−29%** | **100%** |

The photonics growth trajectory is structurally decoupled from the handset cycle, providing Soitec with a partial hedge that did not exist at scale in prior downturns. Whether that hedge becomes a meaningful revenue contributor at the group level — rather than a high-growth but sub-scale offset — depends on the pace of hyperscaler silicon photonics adoption and the degree to which Soitec's substrate specifications remain the design-of-record across competing foundry SiPho flows. The commercial momentum through H1 FY2026 suggests the answer is affirmative, but the disclosed revenue base remains too small to fully absorb a mobile downturn of the magnitude Soitec experienced in 2023–2025. The customer ecosystem is, in that sense, exactly as diversified as the revenue mix: genuinely broadening, but not yet balanced.

chapters.title: The Moat and Its Limits: Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, and the Engineered Substrate Competitive Landscape
chapters.body:
## A Market Defined by Its Absence of Competition

The first analytical error in assessing Soitec's competitive position is to treat it as a participant in the global silicon wafer market. It is not. The five companies that dominate commodity silicon wafer supply — Shin-Etsu Chemical, SUMCO, GlobalWafers, Siltronic, and SK Siltron — collectively held approximately 82 percent of worldwide silicon wafer revenue as of 2025, measured by the Japan-dominated polished and epitaxial wafer segments that go into logic, memory, and power devices. Soitec competes in none of those segments. Its entire output consists of engineered heterostructure substrates: wafers in which a crystalline layer has been separated from a donor material and bonded to a dissimilar carrier via Smart Cut™ ion-implantation transfer. That distinction is not semantics.
