In FD-SOI, RF-SOI, and POI substrates — the three platforms that collectively generate the vast majority of Soitec's revenue — independent market analysts credited Soitec with above 90 percent share of commercial supply through at least 2025. In POI specifically, commercial-scale production was, as of the frozen snapshot date, essentially synonymous with Soitec's Singapore facility.

That near-monopoly position did not arise from acquisition or regulatory protection. It emerged from the physics of the Smart Cut™ process itself. Ion implantation at the precisely controlled doses and energies required to cleave a defect-free crystalline layer — with defect densities below 0.05 per square centimetre at 22-nanometre FD-SOI geometries — requires deep process knowledge that accumulated at Soitec's Bernin facility over more than three decades. No standard epitaxial deposition or thermal oxidation process can replicate that outcome. This is the bedrock of the moat.

## The Shin-Etsu Paradox: Partner, Shareholder, and Notional Rival

The most nuanced competitive dynamic in Soitec's ecosystem involves Japan's Shin-Etsu Handotai — itself the world's largest producer of commodity silicon wafers and a subsidiary of the broader Shin-Etsu Chemical group. In 1997, Shin-Etsu Handotai signed a cross-licensing agreement with Soitec, gaining rights to manufacture SOI wafers using Smart Cut™ technology. That agreement simultaneously validated the IP — a major Japanese industrial group did not sign a license without technical due diligence — and opened access to the Japanese market for Soitec's wafers. SEH subsequently acquired a minority equity stake in Soitec and retained a board presence through Satoshi Onishi, former CEO of Shin-Etsu Handotai Europe.

On paper, Shin-Etsu's license makes it a potential competitor. In practice, the two companies operate in distinct tiers of the SOI market. SEH's SOI production using Smart Cut™ has historically served the lower-value segments of the market: bulk SOI for MEMS sensors, power management devices, and legacy CMOS nodes where the buried oxide thickness is less critical and wafer uniformity requirements are less stringent. Soitec retained the higher-value tiers — FD-SOI wafers with sub-nanometre silicon layer thickness uniformity for sub-28-nanometre logic nodes, high-resistivity RF-SOI for switch and LNA applications, and POI for piezoelectric filter substrates — where the yield and process control requirements exceed what SEH chose to invest in replicating. The board representation reinforces alignment over competition: a shareholder with a director's-level view of Soitec's order book, customer relationships, and process roadmap has limited commercial incentive to enter markets that would simply destroy joint value. The SEH relationship is better characterised as a structural deterrent to Soitec seeking a second-source arrangement with a hostile competitor than as an actual competitive threat to Soitec's core revenue streams.

## POI: A Substrate Without a Credible Alternative

The competitive analysis of Soitec's POI business requires a brief excursion into RF filter physics. The dominant approaches to manufacturing RF bandpass filters for mobile communications are surface-acoustic-wave (SAW) on bulk lithium tantalate or lithium niobate, and bulk-acoustic-wave (BAW) on thin-film piezoelectric layers deposited on silicon substrates. BAW filter manufacturers — Qorvo, Broadcom (AVAGO heritage), TDK/EPCOS, and Murata — can in principle fabricate their resonator stacks on conventional deposited aluminium nitride films without requiring POI substrates. BAW on deposited AlN was the dominant technology through the first generation of 5G Sub-6 GHz filter rollouts.

The manufacturing argument for POI becomes compelling at 5G mmWave frequencies and above, where filter selectivity requirements demand tighter electromechanical coupling coefficients and lower acoustic loss than deposited thin films deliver at commercial yields. POI's single-crystal piezoelectric layer, transferred via Smart Cut™ from a bulk lithium tantalate or lithium niobate donor, provides a crystallographic uniformity across a 300-millimetre substrate that no chemical vapour deposition of a polycrystalline film can match. The yield advantage at scale translates directly to cost-per-resonator in high-band 5G filter stacks. As of the frozen snapshot, no competitor had demonstrated a credible POI-equivalent substrate at commercial production volumes. Soitec's long-term high-volume supply agreement with Qualcomm Technologies for POI wafers destined for the RF360 front-end module programme — combined with the doubling of Singapore facility capacity to approximately two million 300-millimetre-equivalent wafers per year — established a scale and qualification lead that would require years and hundreds of millions of euros to replicate from scratch.

## SmartSiC: Where the Moat Meets a Market in Freefall

Silicon carbide substrates presented a different competitive calculus. The SiC substrate market entering the 2020s was dominated by Wolfspeed (formerly Cree) in the United States, II-VI/Coherent, and Onsemi through its SiCrystal subsidiary in Germany. Soitec's SmartSiC approach — bonding a thin SiC epitaxial layer onto a polycrystalline SiC carrier using a Smart Cut variant — offered a theoretical cost advantage over bulk SiC boule growth, which is energy-intensive, slow, and prone to micropipe and stacking-fault defects. The thesis was that Smart Cut's layer-transfer efficiency could reduce the donor SiC consumed per device wafer, lowering substrate cost as electric vehicle inverter demand scaled.

What that thesis did not fully price was the velocity of Chinese market entry. SICC, TianYu, and other government-backed Chinese entrants began scaling SiC substrate production in 2023–2024 with cost structures underwritten by state subsidies, and their pricing reached levels that compressed the commercial window for SmartSiC's cost advantage before the technology had reached the volume ramp needed to demonstrate it. Soitec recorded a €41 million impairment of SmartSiC non-current assets in H1 FY2026, triggering a 28.7 percent single-day share price decline on 20 November 2025. The competitive threat in SiC was not a technology challenge — Smart Cut's applicability to SiC layer transfer is well-established — but a pricing-war dynamic that eroded the addressable margin before commercialisation.

## The Patent Estate: Depth, Renewal, and the Expiry Question

Soitec's intellectual property position across its core substrate markets is unusually deep for a company of its size. The Smart Cut™ patent estate was built from the original 1992 filings by founders André-Jacques Auberton-Hervé and Jean-Michel Lamure, and has been continuously refreshed through active R&D. CTO Christophe Maleville held approximately 30 individual patents as of 2025. The company filed approximately 18 new patents in FY2024–FY2025 alone, targeting defect density reduction below 0.05 defects per square centimetre — the threshold required for FD-SOI manufacturability at 22-nanometre nodes — as well as improvements in POI layer uniformity and RF-SOI trap-rich layer optimisation.

The concern that the original 1992–1997 patents are expiring or expired is technically correct but commercially overstated. Patent expirations matter most when the underlying process cannot be improved and when knowledge of the technique is sufficient to reproduce it. Neither condition holds for Soitec's advanced product tiers. The original Smart Cut™ concept — ion implantation followed by molecular bonding and thermal cleaving — is now in the public domain. But the specific recipes for achieving defect-free FD-SOI silicon layers at 6-nanometre thickness with sub-angstrom uniformity, or for transferring lithium tantalate films at temperatures compatible with silicon wafer handling, are embodied in current-generation patents and in tacit process knowledge that does not reside in any published document. The renewal cadence of 18 filings per year ensures that the operative claims protecting Soitec's revenue-generating products remain well within their 20-year patent term.

## The Entrant Problem: Capital, Qualification, and Customer Incumbency

| Barrier | Estimated Magnitude | Key Constraint |
|---|---|---|
| Process development | 5–10 years from concept | Ion implantation recipe and bonding chemistry |
| Clean-room capital | €300–500 million | Comparable to Soitec's Bernin I/II combined footprint |
| Foundry qualification | 12–24 months per customer | Destructive testing at each process node |
| Customer incumbency | Long-term supply agreements | 3–5 year volume contracts with take-or-pay structures |
| IP clearance | 30-year portfolio, 18 new filings/year | Design-around cost plus litigation exposure |

A new entrant attempting to replicate Soitec's RF-SOI or FD-SOI capability would face each of these barriers sequentially, not in parallel. Capital could theoretically be assembled — China's government-backed semiconductor industry has demonstrated the ability to commit several hundred million euros to substrate projects, including entities such as Shen Zhen Xinyuan Semiconductor working in the SOI space. But capital solves only the third or fourth barrier on the list. Process knowledge must be developed or licensed; without Soitec's cooperation, the licensing route is closed, and independent development would take the better part of a decade against an incumbent continuously advancing its defect density and layer uniformity targets. Foundry qualification then adds another 12 to 24 months of destructive testing per customer, during which the incumbent retains the supply relationship. And throughout this period, Soitec's long-term volume agreements with GlobalFoundries, STMicroelectronics, TSMC, and Qualcomm provide customers with little commercial incentive to qualify a second source absent a supply security concern. Chinese SOI development programmes represent a credible medium-term intelligence and technology risk, particularly given the willingness of the Chinese government to absorb decade-long qualification timelines to establish domestic supply. But as of the frozen snapshot date, no Chinese entrant had demonstrated FD-SOI or RF-SOI substrates at commercial yield levels sufficient to initiate foundry qualification at a Tier 1 customer. The moat was intact. Its durability across a ten-year horizon against a well-funded state-directed programme was a less settled question.

chapters.title: Timeline and Forward Catalysts: From SmartSiC Impairment to the 6G Substrate Cycle
chapters.body:
## The Eight-Month Sequence That Remade Soitec

The catalyst arc that has defined Soitec's investment thesis since late 2025 began not with a financial disclosure but with a personnel announcement. On 1 October 2025, the company confirmed that Pierre Barnabé — CEO since 2017 and the architect of the company's scaling from roughly €500 million in annual revenue to the FY2023 peak of €1.09 billion — would depart effective 31 March 2026. The announcement landed without a named successor, immediately raising questions about whether the resignation reflected board pressure over the accelerating mobile downturn, a strategic disagreement over the SmartSiC capital commitment, or a planned succession after nine years. The market's unease was visible: shares slipped on the news, though the larger reckoning remained seven weeks away.

That reckoning arrived on [19 November 2025](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/11/19/3191252/0/en/SOITEC-SOITEC-REPORTS-SECOND-QUARTER-REVENUE-AND-HALF-YEAR-RESULTS-OF-FISCAL-YEAR-2026.html), when Soitec released H1 FY2026 results. The headline numbers were stark: revenue of €231 million for the six months to 30 September 2025, a 29 percent organic decline year-on-year; a net loss of €67 million against a €14 million profit in H1 FY2025; and, most consequentially, a €41 million impairment of SmartSiC non-current assets reflecting a downward revision to silicon carbide market prospects driven by aggressive pricing from Chinese SiC entrants. Soitec's shares fell 28.7 percent in a single session on 20 November 2025 — the sharpest single-day decline in years — erasing roughly a quarter of the company's market capitalisation and compressing the stock to levels last seen before the pandemic-era semiconductor boom. The impairment was not merely an accounting entry; it signalled that the EV power-electronics thesis that had motivated hundreds of millions of euros of SmartSiC investment was, at minimum, severely time-shifted.

The board moved decisively to fill the leadership vacuum. On [8 January 2026](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/01/08/3215061/0/en/SOITEC-BOARD-OF-DIRECTORS-APPOINTS-LAURENT-R%C3%89MONT-CHIEF-EXECUTIVE-OFFICER-EFFECTIVE-APRIL-2026.html), it announced Laurent Rémont — formerly Senior Vice President for Radio Frequency and Sensors at Infineon Technologies — as the incoming CEO, effective 1 April 2026. Rémont's appointment carried a deliberate strategic signal: his background spanning STMicroelectronics (an FD-SOI co-developer and anchor customer), Kontron, and Infineon RF semiconductors positioned him as a commercial and product-strategy executive rather than a process-technology founder. He joined as special adviser on 16 March 2026, giving him a two-week overlap with Barnabé before formally assuming the CEO role on 1 April 2026, subject to ratification as a board director at the Annual General Meeting expected in July 2026.

Sandwiched between those leadership events, on 3 February 2026, Soitec released its Q3 FY2026 revenue announcement. The company had guided for mid-to-high single-digit sequential organic growth from the Q2 FY2026 base of €139 million — a modest but directionally important inflection after the H1 trough, suggesting the worst of the mobile-inventory correction was passing and that POI shipment volumes were beginning to recover.

## The 27 May Inflection Point

The next major catalyst as of the frozen snapshot date — 27 May 2026 — is the Q4 revenue and full-year FY2026 results disclosure. It falls four days after this snapshot's freeze but represents the single most consequential near-term data point for the recovery thesis. Investors will be scrutinising three dimensions simultaneously.

First, **Mobile Communications segment volume recovery**: the segment contributed €119 million in H1 FY2026 (down 30 percent year-on-year) and the trajectory of Q3 and Q4 RF-SOI and POI wafer shipments will determine whether the sequential inflection has broadened into a sustainable ramp. The GlobalFoundries 9SW platform qualification and the continued TSMC RF-SOI pull from Qualcomm and MediaTek designs are the operational levers; any management commentary confirming volume binding above the Q2 trough would materially upgrade the FY2027 earnings bridge.

Second, **POI as a separate disclosure line**: Soitec has not historically broken out POI wafer volumes or revenue as a standalone segment metric. Any move toward greater POI transparency — volume shipped to Qualcomm's RF360 programme, revenue contribution as a share of Mobile Communications, or Singapore-specific capacity utilisation — would be treated as a positive catalyst by analysts attempting to model the filter-substrate upgrade cycle. The Singapore Pasir Ris expansion specifically allocated incremental clean-room capacity to POI production, and the long-term volume agreements with both Qualcomm and MediaTek provide contractual underpinning; the question is whether management chooses 27 May as the moment to quantify that ramp for the market.

Third, **Edge and Cloud AI growth durability**: the segment grew 34 percent organically in H1 FY2026 despite a broader revenue contraction, driven by Photonics-SOI demand from hyperscaler optical-transceiver programmes and FD-SOI traction in automotive ADAS and edge inference. A deceleration here — even modest — would remove the growth narrative's only unambiguous positive data point; continuation above 20 percent organically would reinforce the argument that Soitec's diversification into AI-adjacent substrates is structurally, not cyclically, driven.

## The SmartSiC Fork

Rémont's first substantive strategic communication — whether at the 27 May results or the July AGM — will address the SmartSiC question that the €41 million impairment left unresolved. Three paths exist, each with materially different capital and earnings implications.

| Strategic option | Capex implication | EBITDA trajectory | Narrative |
|---|---|---|---|
| Continue at reduced pace pending SiC recovery | Moderate ongoing spend; €20–40M annually | Margin drag persists 2–3 years | Optionality preserved; credibility risk if market recovery delayed further |
| License SmartSiC IP to SiC device makers | Near-zero incremental capex | Royalty line adds 2–4 points to EBITDA margin | Reframes SmartSiC as an IP asset, not a failed bet |
| Full exit; reallocate capex to RF-SOI and POI | Capex freed for Mobile and AI substrate lines | Fastest path to margin normalisation | Cleanest break; risks writing off remaining SiC asset value |

Rémont's Infineon biography — a company that has invested heavily in SiC power semiconductors as a device manufacturer, not a substrate supplier — gives him an unusually informed vantage point on the competitive dynamics that triggered the impairment. His decision will reveal whether the board sees SmartSiC as a temporarily impaired growth option or a strategic cul-de-sac.

## The 6G Long Cycle

Beyond the near-term recovery, a structural catalyst is assembling in plain sight. The 6G standardisation process, with commercial deployment targeted in the 2028–2030 window, is already shaping RF front-end architecture requirements at Nokia Bell Labs, Ericsson Research, and Samsung Research. The frequency bands under exploration — sub-THz, spanning 100 GHz to 300 GHz — impose material constraints that rule out commodity silicon and conventional III-V platforms. At these frequencies, gallium nitride-on-silicon (Soitec's RF-GaN substrate) and advanced high-resistivity RF-SOI are among the only commercially scalable material platforms with the electron mobility and isolation characteristics required for power-efficient amplification.

The substrate-content-per-device trajectory reinforces the structural case. The migration from 4G to 5G Sub-6 GHz roughly doubled the RF front-end module complexity; the further migration to 5G mmWave added POI-based BAW filters in significant quantities. If 6G front-ends require comparable step-changes — more bands, higher isolation, tighter linearity — the addressable substrate revenue per handset shipped increases independently of unit volume growth. For Soitec, this means that even in a scenario of flat global smartphone unit sales through 2030, revenue per unit shipped should rise meaningfully, providing a structural volume tailwind that compounds the cyclical recovery already underway in the RF-SOI and POI product lines.

The 27 May results will not resolve the 6G question — that is a 2027–2028 story. But they will establish whether the foundation from which Soitec intends to participate in that cycle is recovering on the schedule the investment thesis requires.

chapters.title: Smart Cut as Institutional DNA: The IP Estate, CEA-Leti Collaboration, and R&D Architecture
chapters.body:
## The Patent Estate: Ion Implantation to Institutional Permanence

When André-Jacques Auberton-Hervé and Jean-Michel Lamure filed the foundational patents for the Smart Cut™ process between 1992 and 1997, they were protecting something deceptively simple: a method of cleaving and transferring an ultra-thin crystalline layer from a donor wafer to an insulating substrate using light-ion implantation and molecular adhesion bonding. Those core filings — covering the fundamental physics of hydrogen-ion bombardment, thermally induced micro-fracture, and direct wafer bonding — constituted the original moat. Several of those patents have now expired or are approaching expiry after the standard twenty-year term, a fact that competitors have periodically cited as evidence of a diminishing defensive perimeter.

The characterisation misreads the architecture of Soitec's intellectual property position. The original core patents were always the seed, not the harvest. Over the following three decades, Soitec built a layered continuation estate covering process improvements, specific material system adaptations — including the lithium tantalate and lithium niobate transfers that underpin POI (Piezoelectric-on-Insulator) substrates, and the SiC variant at the heart of SmartSiC™ — defect density reduction techniques, buried-oxide thickness uniformity methods, and equipment configuration innovations that collectively make the process manufacturable at commercial yield rather than merely demonstrable in a laboratory. The company filed approximately 18 new patents in FY2024–FY2025 alone, specifically targeting defect densities below 0.05 defects per square centimetre for FD-SOI applications, a threshold relevant for qualifying 22 nm and 18 nm process nodes at STMicroelectronics and Samsung Foundry.

Chief Technology Officer Christophe Maleville, who joined Soitec in 1993 — one year after its founding — holds approximately 30 personal patents and has authored or co-authored more than 30 published papers on SOI process development. That biography is not incidental detail; it is the human expression of the estate's architecture. Maleville was present for the first commercial wafer deliveries, for the transition from 150 mm to 200 mm to 300 mm platforms, for the adaptation of Smart Cut™ to piezoelectric materials, and for the development of SmartSiC. His continuity through the April 2026 CEO transition — while four of nine executive committee members are relative newcomers — provides a form of institutional IP governance that no succession document can replicate.

## CEA-Leti: The Three-Kilometre Partnership

The relationship between Soitec and CEA-Leti, the microelectronics research laboratory of the French Atomic Energy Commission situated roughly three kilometres from the Bernin fabrication campus, predates Soitec itself. Smart Cut™ was invented within CEA-Leti's walls before it was transferred to the company that would industrialise it. That origin story shaped an unusually durable institutional entanglement: the two organisations have maintained continuous joint research programmes since the early 1990s, covering successive generations of SOI node development and, more recently, POI material optimisation for bulk-acoustic-wave filter applications.

The collaboration is formalised through both research agreements and equity. CEA Investissement — the investment arm of the Atomic Energy Commission — held a 7.21% stake in Soitec and occupied a board seat as of the frozen snapshot date, with Julie Galland, Director of Technological Research at CEA, serving as the designated board representative. [Soitec IR / Board of Directors](https://www.soitec.com/home/investors/governance/board-of-directors) That directorship gives CEA a voice in capital allocation decisions and, implicitly, in the pace of licensing any jointly developed IP. The practical consequence is that Soitec's R&D roadmap and CEA-Leti's research agenda remain tightly synchronised: CEA-Leti provides access to advanced research nodes — including sub-10 nm process equipment that Soitec does not itself own — while Soitec contributes volume manufacturing insight and co-funds programmes aligned to its commercial pipeline.

For FD-SOI, the joint programme has focused on the next-generation ultra-thin buried-oxide architectures needed for 18 nm and 12 nm FD-SOI nodes, where buried-oxide thickness must be controlled to within a few nanometres across 300 mm wafers without introducing crystallographic defects. For POI, the collaboration addresses material optimisation for lithium tantalate layer transfer quality, piezoelectric coefficient uniformity, and surface roughness specifications required by BAW filter manufacturers.

## The Global R&D Organisation

Beyond the Bernin campus — where approximately 500 engineers and scientists constitute the core technical workforce — Soitec operates a network of applied R&D and applications-engineering outposts structured around customer proximity. The United States office, centred in San Jose, supports engagement with GlobalFoundries and the broader North American fabless ecosystem. Singapore houses both volume manufacturing for POI and RF-SOI and a local engineering team supporting the Pasir Ris expansion. Offices in Seoul, Tokyo, Hsinchu, Shanghai, and Shenzhen allow direct process qualification dialogue with Samsung Foundry, Renesas, TSMC, UMC, and China's domestic foundry customers respectively.

R&D expenditure historically ran at 8–10% of revenues — a capital-intensity ratio that reflects the substrate business's hybrid character, somewhere between a specialty materials company and a process technology licensor. At the FY2023 revenue peak of approximately €1.09 billion, this translated to €87–109 million annually in R&D spending, a figure that narrowed in absolute terms during the FY2024–FY2026 revenue contraction but was not proportionately cut, consistent with management's stated commitment to protecting the innovation pipeline through the cycle.

## Smart Stacking™ and the 3D Integration Vector

Parallel to Smart Cut™ runs a complementary IP pillar: Smart Stacking™, a process that transfers completed back-end-of-line processed wafers onto new substrates, enabling three-dimensional integration of heterogeneous circuit layers. The technology's historical commercial expression was Imager-SOI, the substrate platform used in back-illuminated CMOS image sensors — a product line being phased out in FY2026 as Sony Semiconductor Solutions internalises its substrate supply. Yet Smart Stacking retains strategic relevance as hyperscalers and AI chip designers explore 3D-integrated accelerator architectures where logic, memory, and photonic layers must be bonded at wafer scale with micron-level alignment.

## The Trade-Secret Dimension: What Cannot Be Filed

The deepest layer of Soitec's competitive moat is also its least visible. No patent covers the specific equipment maintenance schedules, the proprietary defect-inspection algorithms, the bonding surface preparation chemistry optimised over tens of thousands of wafer runs, or the institutional memory embedded in the Bernin operations workforce — some of whom have operated the same tool sets since the Bernin 1 hall opened in 1999. This accumulated process know-how cannot be patented because it is not reducible to a novel, non-obvious, and industrially applicable invention; it is, rather, the aggregate of thirty years of trial-and-error learning encoded in standard operating procedures, training programmes, and the tacit knowledge of experienced process engineers.

A competitor with unlimited capital and the original core patents in hand would still face a five-to-ten year yield learning curve before approaching Soitec's defect density specifications — precisely because those specifications were themselves the product of iterative improvement that no patent discloses. As the original 1992–1997 filings expire, this trade-secret dimension becomes proportionately more important as the residual moat. It is, in a meaningful sense, more durable than any individual patent: a patent expires on a fixed date; the process knowledge embedded in an institution that has operated continuously for over three decades does not.

chapters.title: Six Risks: SiC Impairment, Mobile Concentration, FD-SOI Ecosystem, Geopolitics, FX, and Succession
chapters.body:
## Risk 1 — SmartSiC: A Strategic Overhang That Refuses to Clear

The €41 million impairment charge Soitec recorded against its SmartSiC non-current assets in H1 FY2026 was not merely an accounting adjustment — it was a public admission that the strategic rationale underpinning several years of capital allocation had been overtaken by events. The charge drove a net loss of €67 million for the half-year period ended 30 September 2025 and triggered a 28.7 percent single-day share-price collapse on 20 November 2025 when results were disclosed. Yet the more uncomfortable question for investors is not the impairment itself but what remains on the balance sheet after it, and whether further write-downs are probable.

Soitec had invested heavily through the 2020–2026 period in adapting the Smart Cut™ process to silicon carbide substrates — bonding thin SiC epitaxial layers onto polycrystalline SiC carriers to produce a substrate that promised higher yield and lower defect density than conventional SiC bulk-grown wafers. The thesis was well-constructed at inception: EV penetration was accelerating, SiC power electronics were the preferred architecture for inverters, and Soitec's bonding expertise represented a genuine differentiation. What the company could not fully anticipate was the speed at which Chinese SiC entrants — including SICC, TankeBlue, and Shandong Tianyue — scaled production capacity and drove down substrate pricing on commodity SiC, compressing the addressable premium for a differentiated SmartSiC approach. Post-impairment, the remaining carrying value of SmartSiC assets has not been independently disclosed in granular form, but the scale of the original investment implies residual exposure that remains material. Any further deterioration in SiC substrate pricing — or any delay in SmartSiC achieving commercial volumes — carries a non-trivial probability of triggering incremental charges. New CEO Laurent Rémont faces a binary strategic choice here with little room for equivocation: commit to a premium differentiated positioning that requires additional customer qualification cycles, or accept a licensing-and-IP-harvesting trajectory that caps the upside but stops the cash burn.

## Risk 2 — Mobile Concentration: A Single Architecture Shift Could Dislocate the Volume Base

Approximately 50 to 55 percent of Soitec's revenue derives from RF-SOI and POI wafers supplied into smartphone RF front-end modules, according to the H1 FY2026 segment data, which showed Mobile Communications contributing €119 million — roughly 52 percent of the €231 million total. The concentration within that segment is more acute than the headline number suggests: commercially, the wafers flow primarily through two foundries — GlobalFoundries at its Fab 9 campus in Malta, New York, and TSMC in Hsinchu — which manufacture RF switch and filter die for a handful of fabless chipmakers led by Qualcomm, Skyworks Solutions, Qorvo, and MediaTek. The end-customer pyramid narrows further to Apple and Samsung, whose handset unit volumes ultimately drive foundry loading.

This architecture has a systemic vulnerability. If a major OEM were to redesign its RF front-end to consolidate switch and filter functions into a bulk-CMOS die — a direction being explored, if not yet commercially validated, by several fabless players — Soitec's wafer volumes could fall structurally rather than cyclically. Similarly, if GlobalFoundries were to exit the RF-SOI business or repurpose Fab 9 capacity (following its 2023 decision to abandon 7 nm advanced logic), Soitec would face a foundry concentration risk that long-term supply agreements cannot fully hedge. The probability of these dislocations is low within a three-to-five year window but non-negligible over a decade. The magnitude, however, would be severe: a 20 percent structural decline in RF-SOI volumes at current price points would reduce revenues by roughly €80–100 million annually at trough scale — equivalent to wiping out most of the Automotive & Industrial and a significant portion of the Edge & Cloud AI segments in dollar terms.

## Risk 3 — FD-SOI: An Ecosystem That Runs Through Two Foundries

FD-SOI's commercial viability depends almost entirely on STMicroelectronics and Samsung Foundry continuing to invest in and commercially promote their respective 28 nm and 22 nm FD-SOI nodes. STMicroelectronics, which co-developed FD-SOI with Soitec and CEA-Leti and operates the primary volume line at Crolles, France, announced a broad restructuring in early 2025 that includes headcount reductions and a reassessment of capacity at Crolles. If ST were to curtail FD-SOI production — either by retiring the 28 nm node earlier than anticipated or by redirecting Crolles clean-room space to silicon carbide (ST is an aggressive SiC IDM in its own right) — there is no alternative foundry currently positioned to absorb FD-SOI volume at commercial scale. Samsung's 28FDS node at Giheung provides a secondary anchor, but Samsung has not publicly committed to advancing FD-SOI beyond 28 nm, and its foundry business has been reorganising under competitive pressure from TSMC's dominant share gains at leading-edge nodes. The FD-SOI ecosystem, in short, is a two-legged stool. One leg wobbling puts the entire structure at risk, and Soitec has limited commercial leverage to force either foundry to sustain or expand commitments it finds uneconomic.

## Risk 4 — Geopolitics and Export Controls: The China Revenue Question

Soitec operates sales and application-engineering offices in Shanghai and Shenzhen and supplies substrates to foundries across Taiwan, South Korea, and, to a lesser extent, China. The precise revenue exposure to China-domiciled customers has not been publicly disaggregated in Soitec's financial disclosures with the specificity that US-listed peers are required to provide under SEC rules. However, the risk vector is clear: US Bureau of Industry and Security export control rules — extended and tightened several times since 2022 — govern the re-export of advanced semiconductors and, increasingly, the semiconductor materials and substrates required to manufacture them. Were BIS to classify certain advanced SOI substrates as controlled items requiring export licences for China-bound supply chains, Soitec's ability to serve Chinese foundries or end customers would be constrained. The CHIPS Act ecosystem further creates indirect pressure: US-subsidised foundries and their supply chains face guardrails on China technology transfer, which could cascade upstream into substrate procurement requirements. Soitec's Singapore facility — geographically and politically distinct from France — provides some jurisdictional flexibility, but Singapore-origin goods remain subject to US re-export rules if they incorporate US-origin technology or exceed certain thresholds.

## Risk 5 — Foreign Exchange: The Euro Strengthens, the Margin Compresses

Soitec reports in euros, but its long-term wafer supply agreements are typically priced in US dollars or indexed to USD benchmarks — a legacy of the global semiconductor industry's dollar-denominated pricing conventions. The H1 FY2026 income statement revealed a €19 million foreign-exchange loss as the euro appreciated against the dollar during the period, compressing reported revenue and EBITDA beyond what volume declines alone would explain. At the full-year scale implied by the trailing twelve months through September 2025 — approximately €784 million in revenue — a sustained 5 percent euro strengthening would reduce reported revenues by roughly €35–40 million without any change in volumes or pricing. Soitec's Singapore operations provide a partial natural hedge: Singapore dollar costs and USD revenues within the Pasir Ris facility create an offset at the entity level, and the company disclosed a hedging policy using forward contracts on a portion of its USD revenue exposure. But the hedge coverage ratio and tenor have not been publicly detailed, and currency moves of the magnitude seen in the 2024–2026 period — driven by diverging Federal Reserve and ECB policy trajectories — can overwhelm short-dated hedges. The margin sensitivity is non-linear near the trough: at €580–620 million in full-year FY2026 revenues, a €10 million FX headwind represents approximately 1.5 percentage points of EBITDA margin, a material swing when the company is trying to demonstrate a recovery narrative.

## Risk 6 — CEO Transition: Eighteen Months That Will Define the Recovery Trajectory

Laurent Rémont formally assumed the CEO role on 1 April 2026, having spent approximately six weeks as a special adviser before the handover from Pierre Barnabé. His biography is directly relevant — more than fifteen years at STMicroelectronics, including exposure to FD-SOI process development, followed by the SVP RF and Sensors role at Infineon — but relevant is not the same as prepared for the specific decisions that will land in his inbox within the first twelve to eighteen months. The SmartSiC strategic resolution — persist, license, or curtail — requires a judgment about SiC market structure that hinges on reading Chinese competitor cost curves and Soitec's own manufacturing readiness, a domain where Rémont has no direct prior experience. The FY2027 capital expenditure planning cycle will require him to make commitments on capacity additions before the mobile recovery is fully confirmed, risking either under-investment in a snapback or over-investment at the trough. And the Qualcomm POI supply agreement — the volume anchor for the Singapore expansion — will at some point require renegotiation; the terms, pricing, and duration of any renewal will be among the most consequential decisions of Rémont's early tenure. Barnabé's resignation preceded the H1 FY2026 impairment announcement by six weeks, a sequencing that raised market questions about whether departing management had fully priced the SiC downside into the balance sheet before handing over. Rémont has every incentive to conduct a thorough strategic review and, if necessary, take additional charges early in his tenure — a kitchen-sink first half — to establish clean baselines. That discipline, if exercised promptly, would reduce the overhang; the risk is that a new CEO underestimates the depth of the SmartSiC write-down still required, leaving residual impairment risk to resurface later and undermining the recovery narrative he is tasked with delivering.

chapters.title: The $2 Billion Ambition: POI Ramp, 6G Architecture, and the 2026–2030 Horizon
chapters.body:

To reach the target by FY2028, the company needed to sustain a compound annual revenue growth rate of approximately 27 percent from the FY2025 base; by FY2029, approximately 20 percent annualised. Neither figure was outlandish by Soitec's own historical standards: the FY2021–FY2023 expansion, when 5G handset penetration was accelerating and the Singapore fab was in full ramp, had delivered a 37 percent CAGR, carrying revenue from €583.76 million to €1.09 billion in two fiscal years.

The critical distinction between that supercycle and the anticipated recovery arc lay in the nature of the demand signal. The earlier surge was driven by a one-time technology migration — 4G-to-5G handset replacement — compressed by a post-pandemic device upgrade surge. The forward path to $2 billion rested on a more diversified and arguably more durable set of structural drivers: POI volume uplift from the Singapore expansion, continued RF-SOI content-per-device growth as mmWave architectures penetrated mid-tier handsets, and compounding growth in edge AI and silicon-photonics substrates. The key variable was whether long-term supply agreements — typically three-to-five-year volume commitments with tier-one foundry and fabless customers — could underwrite the trajectory with sufficient predictability to support the margin expansion the ambition required.

## POI: Singapore as the Revenue Engine

The most concrete pillar of the medium-term case was the Pasir Ris capacity expansion. Soitec had completed the extension of its Singapore wafer-fabrication facility in 2024–2025, doubling annual production capacity to roughly two million 300 mm-equivalent wafers per year. The expansion was not speculative: [long-term high-volume manufacturing agreements with Qualcomm Technologies](https://www.soitec.com/home/investors/regulated-information/financial-reports--results-other-regulated-releases) — for POI wafers feeding Qualcomm's RF360 front-end module production — and MediaTek anchored the capacity commitment with contractual revenue underwriting that most capital-heavy semiconductor investments lacked at inception.

The revenue leverage embedded in full Singapore utilisation was substantial. With POI wafers commanding a pricing premium over standard RF-SOI substrates — reflecting both the piezoelectric-layer transfer complexity and Soitec's near-monopoly position in high-volume POI supply — a full-utilisation run-rate implied a POI revenue contribution potentially reaching €400–500 million annually by FY2028–FY2029, versus a contribution that remained unquantified in segment disclosures but was clearly sub-€150 million in FY2025 given the product's still-nascent commercial stage. The filter-count escalation in 5G architectures reinforced the addressable market expansion: 5G Sub-6 GHz handsets carried approximately 70–100 RF filters per device; 5G mmWave architectures required substantially higher counts for additional frequency bands, while early 6G reference architectures circulating among Qualcomm and Ericsson standardisation teams envisioned further increases in filter stages per RF front-end module. Even at flat global handset unit volumes, a steady migration from Sub-6 GHz to mmWave added incremental POI wafer demand per phone shipped — lifting Soitec's revenue per device without requiring market share gains.

## Edge and Cloud AI: The Structural Backstop

If POI represented the cyclical recovery driver, the Edge and Cloud AI segment provided the diversification that gave the $2 billion ambition its resilience. The segment had grown [34 percent organically in the first half of FY2026](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/11/19/3191252/0/en/SOITEC-SOITEC-REPORTS-SECOND-QUARTER-REVENUE-AND-HALF-YEAR-RESULTS-OF-FISCAL-YEAR-2026.html) — the only major segment to expand during the trough — reflecting dual tailwinds: FD-SOI adoption for always-on edge inference and Photonics-SOI demand from hyperscaler AI data-centre buildouts.

The FD-SOI power-efficiency advantage — approximately 30–40 percent lower active power consumption versus equivalent bulk CMOS at 28 nm — had become increasingly decisive as automotive OEMs and industrial-edge designers faced tightening thermal budgets for ADAS processing. STMicroelectronics, the primary FD-SOI foundry customer and Soitec's closest technology partner, was actively expanding its 28 nm and 22 nm FD-SOI capacity at Crolles for automotive and industrial customers. The silicon-photonics subsegment was meanwhile benefiting directly from the hyperscaler AI capex supercycle: optical transceiver ASICs handling 400G and 800G cluster interconnects inside the AI training facilities of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon used Photonics-SOI wafers with waveguide-optimised parameters that only Soitec could supply at scale. Modelling the segment at even a conservative 20–25 percent annualised growth rate from the approximately €192 million annualised run-rate implied by H1 FY2026, the Edge and Cloud AI segment could contribute €350–420 million to group revenue by FY2029 — a meaningful structural offset to any shortfall in the mobile recovery trajectory.

## RF-SOI Normalisation and the mmWave Step-Change

The Q2 FY2026 sequential revenue recovery of 47 percent across the Mobile Communications segment signalled that the two-year handset inventory correction had substantively run its course. The more strategically important question was what the post-correction RF-SOI baseline looked like as mmWave architectures began to penetrate beyond premium US handsets.

Through 2025, 5G mmWave remained concentrated in premium Apple and Samsung devices aimed at Verizon and AT&T millimetre-wave networks. The incremental volume from a mid-tier mmWave migration — expected to accelerate from 2027 as Qualcomm's mmWave modem costs declined — represented a meaningful average selling price step-up for Soitec: mmWave RF front-ends required more RF-SOI switch die per handset, lifting revenue-per-device from the Sub-6 GHz baseline. Early 6G standardisation, which the ITU's IMT-2030 framework expected to see commercially deployed from 2030, further extended the content-per-device upgrade cycle. For Soitec, whose RF-SOI economics depended not on handset unit volumes but on the architectural complexity of the RF front-end, this structural upgrade path mattered more than market share dynamics between Apple and its Android peers.

## SmartSiC: Toward a Licensing Resolution

The SmartSiC impairment closed one chapter without eliminating the underlying intellectual property asset. Soitec's Smart Cut variant for silicon carbide remained a technically differentiated approach to improving SiC substrate yield and cost, and the €41 million write-down reflected a market-timing miscalculation — Chinese producers compressing the pricing environment faster than management had modelled — rather than a technology failure per se.

[Laurent Rémont's Infineon background](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/01/08/3215061/0/en/SOITEC-BOARD-OF-DIRECTORS-APPOINTS-LAURENT-R%C3%89MONT-CHIEF-EXECUTIVE-OFFICER-EFFECTIVE-APRIL-2026.html) provided a specific lens for evaluating the licensing route. During his tenure leading Infineon's Radio Frequency and Sensors division, Rémont had operated a business unit heavily dependent on the performance and cost trajectory of third-party specialty substrates. More pointedly, Infineon's CoolSiC MOSFET franchise — one of the leading SiC power device platforms for EV inverters — was itself a potential licensing partner: the substrate cost reduction that SmartSiC's bonding approach could deliver would directly improve Infineon's SiC device margins. Similar logic applied to Wolfspeed, onsemi, and STMicroelectronics, each managing SiC substrate supply chains under ongoing price pressure from Chinese competitors. A royalty model, rather than a volume manufacturing play, would allow Soitec to monetise decades of SiC IP development without committing further capital to a market whose cost structure had been fundamentally disrupted.

## The Capital Return Question

Perhaps the most underappreciated element of Soitec's 2026 financial position was the gap between its balance sheet strength and its market valuation. At September 2025, the company held [€808 million in cash](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/11/19/3191252/0/en/SOITEC-SOITEC-REPORTS-SECOND-QUARTER-REVENUE-AND-HALF-YEAR-RESULTS-OF-FISCAL-YEAR-2026.html) against net debt of only €145 million — and the gross cash position alone represented approximately 40 percent of a post-impairment market capitalisation compressed by the November 2025 share-price shock. With capex normalising to approximately €140 million per year following Singapore's completion and free cash flow inflecting positive in FY2026, the question of capital allocation became increasingly acute.

The French state-linked anchor shareholders — Bpifrance Participations at 11.49 percent and CEA Investissement at 7.21 percent — created a distinctive incentive calculus. Both institutions carried mandates well beyond financial return maximisation: Bpifrance, the French public investment bank, and CEA Investissement, the commercialisation arm of the institution that originally developed Smart Cut, were structurally oriented toward technology sovereignty and industrial employment. In a conventional shareholder structure dominated by return-seeking capital, a buyback at trough multiples would have been straightforward given the cash position relative to market capitalisation. With two founding-era state entities holding board seats and combined control of nearly 20 percent of the vote, however, deploying surplus capital toward technology-sovereignty programmes — accelerating FD-SOI ecosystem development, backing European 6G substrate R&D, or co-investing with CEA-Leti in next-generation heterostructure platforms — carried institutional logic that a pure financial return framework would miss.

That tension — between buyback and reinvestment, between capital efficiency and strategic sovereignty, between Rémont's return-focused semiconductor operating background and the French state's technology-industrial priorities — was the defining governance question as Soitec entered the second half of the decade. The $2 billion ambition was achievable. The path to achieving it, and who ultimately captured the value created along the way, was the more interesting question.

financials.key_finding: Soitec is a mid-cap specialty materials company with peak-cycle revenue of €1.09 billion (FY2023, ending March 2023) and a current trough of roughly €780–800 million on a trailing-twelve-month basis through late 2025. The FY2025 (year ended 31 March 2025) result of €890.85 million represented an 8.9 percent decline year-on-year, itself following a 10.2 percent decline in FY2024 — a two-year down-cycle driven primarily by the mobile communications RF front-end inventory correction and downstream smartphone unit softness. The H1 FY2026 result of €231 million (29 percent organic decline year-on-year) confirmed the trough extended into the fiscal first half ending September 2025, with a €41 million SmartSiC impairment charge driving a net loss of €67 million versus a €14 million profit in H1 FY2025. EBITDA margins have proven resilient at 33–34 percent through the down-cycle, reflecting the company's high fixed-cost absorption at lower volumes partially offset by wafer cost efficiency. Free cash flow turned positive in FY2025 at €26 million (versus negative €43 million in FY2024) as capital expenditure normalised after the Singapore fab build-out peak. The capital structure is conservative: shareholders' equity stood at €1.6 billion and net financial debt was only €94 million as of 31 March 2025, with a cash position of €808 million against total financial debt of €953 million as of 30 September 2025, yielding a net debt-to-LTM-EBITDA ratio of approximately 0.5 times. The company's medium-term revenue target is $2 billion (approximately €1.85 billion at 2026 exchange rates) with roughly 40 percent EBITDA margin, implying a near-doubling from trough revenues, underpinned by POI volume ramp, RF-SOI 5G upgrade cycle continuation, and edge/cloud AI substrate growth.
structural_observations: Revenue base and cycle: Annual revenue peaked at €1.09 billion in FY2023 (ended March 2023) driven by the 5G smartphone supercycle; declined to €977.91 million in FY2024 and €890.85 million in FY2025; trailing-twelve-month revenue through September 2025 approximately €784 million; FY2021 revenue was €583.76 million and FY2022 was €862.74 million, indicating a high-growth phase (FY21–FY23 CAGR ~37%) followed by a two-year correction. Revenue trajectory is volume-driven (long-term supply agreements) rather than spot price-driven, making forward revenue more predictable once volumes are contracted.

Fiscal year cadence: Soitec operates a non-calendar fiscal year ending 31 March, reporting two half-year revenue and P&L disclosures (H1 in November; full year in May) and quarterly revenue-only disclosures; H1 FY2026 revenue €231 million (H1 ended September 30, 2025); H2 FY2026 guidance implied sequential recovery in Q3 and ~20% sequential growth in Q4, suggesting full-year FY2026 of approximately €580–620 million based on public guidance as of February 2026.

Margin progression: EBITDA margin sustained above 30% through the down-cycle — 33.5% in FY2025 (full year) and 34.1% in H1 FY2026 — demonstrating the resilience of a specialty materials business model with long-term supply agreements and limited spot-price exposure; EBIT margin compressed to approximately 15% as of Q4 FY2025; net income turned to a loss in H1 FY2026 due primarily to the €41 million SmartSiC impairment and a €19 million foreign-exchange loss, with the adjusted current net result (excluding exceptional items) only marginally negative at approximately €2 million.

Capital structure: Balance sheet is well-capitalised; shareholders' equity €1.6 billion (March 31, 2025, up ~€100 million year-on-year); gross financial debt €782 million (March 2025), rising to €953 million (September 2025) following drawdowns to fund the Singapore expansion; net debt €94 million (March 2025) and €145 million (September 2025); net debt-to-EBITDA approximately 0.5x — significantly below the 2x–3x leverage common in semiconductor capital-intensive peers; the company carries €808 million cash (September 2025), providing capacity to self-fund the remaining Singapore commissioning and the medium-term capex programme estimated at ~€140 million for FY2026.

Capital expenditure trajectory: Capex peaked during the Singapore fab construction phase (FY2023–FY2025); FY2026 capex guidance reduced to approximately €140 million from €150 million prior guidance, signalling a return to maintenance-and-capacity-optimisation spend rather than greenfield construction; free cash flow should inflect positive again in FY2026 as capex falls and volumes recover.

Comparable peers and market context: Soitec is not directly comparable to commodity silicon wafer producers (Shin-Etsu Chemical, SUMCO, Siltronic, GlobalWafers) given its specialty engineered-substrate positioning and structurally higher margins; the closest comparable is a cross between a specialty materials company (e.g., Entegris, CMC Materials) and a semiconductor equipment / substrate supplier; market capitalisation ranged from approximately €3.5 billion to €9 billion over the FY2022–FY2025 period, reflecting high beta to the semiconductor cycle; the stock declined approximately 75 percent from its 2022 peak of roughly €350 per share to approximately €25 per share post the November 2025 H1 FY2026 results announcement.

Segment revenue mix (H1 FY2026): Mobile Communications €119 million (down 30% YoY, ~52% of total); Automotive & Industrial €15 million (down 74% YoY, ~6% of total, heavily impacted by SmartSiC pause and automotive inventory correction); Edge & Cloud AI €96 million (up 34% YoY excluding Imager-SOI phase-out, ~42% of total, reflecting Photonics-SOI and FD-SOI strength); the shift in mix toward Edge & Cloud AI is a structural positive as this segment carries similar or higher margins and is less correlated to the handset unit cycle.

leadership.key_finding: Soitec completed a generational CEO transition on 1 April 2026, as Laurent Rémont, aged 54, assumed the role following nine years under Pierre Barnabé. Rémont brings a directly relevant industrial biography: after more than fifteen years at STMicroelectronics (which co-developed FD-SOI with Soitec and CEA-Leti) in general management and R&D roles, he served as CTO of Kontron AG (embedded computing), then as Senior Vice President at Infineon Technologies leading the Radio Frequency and Sensors division — a business unit that develops MEMS microphones, pressure sensors, and RF components using substrates similar to Soitec's output. His Grenoble INP–ENSERG engineering pedigree places him in the same Isère semiconductor ecosystem where Soitec was founded, and where both CEA-Leti and STMicroelectronics maintain major R&D presence. The board that appointed him is substantively refreshed: Frédéric Lissalde (former BorgWarner CEO, automotive electrification background) became Chairman effective 1 March 2025; CFO Albin Jacquemont joined in May 2025 (previously Group CFO at Inetum, SAUR, and Altran); and Chief Product Officer René Jonker (ex-ams AG, NXP, Nexperia) was appointed in October 2025. The board of 12 members includes representatives from the two founding-era institutional anchors — Bpifrance Participations (11.49% shareholder, represented by Samuel Dalens) and CEA Investissement (7.21% shareholder, represented by Julie Galland, Director of Technological Research at CEA) — as well as Satoshi Onishi (former President and CEO of Shin-Etsu Handotai Europe), reflecting the historical cross-licensing partnership with SEH. There is no private equity sponsor influence; the shareholder register is dominated by long-only institutional investors including Baillie Gifford (11.28%) and BlackRock (8.91%). The board is 60 percent women (excluding employee directors) and 70 percent independent, with an average age of 53.
research_notes_for_writer: Dig into Pierre Barnabé's tenure narrative: he became CEO in 2017 following the company's exit from the diversification phase (solar energy, LED) and oversaw the refocus on core SOI substrates; his nine-year reign saw revenue roughly double from ~€500 million to the FY2023 peak of €1.09 billion; investigate why he resigned — was it succession planning, board pressure over the SmartSiC bet, or the mobile down-cycle — and whether the resignation announcement in October 2025 preceded or followed the SmartSiC impairment decision announced in November 2025.

Explore the Christophe Maleville CTO lineage: Maleville has been at Soitec since 1993 (one year after founding), holds approximately 30 patents, and has 30+ published papers on SOI process development; as the institutional memory of Smart Cut™ commercialisation, his continuity through the CEO transition provides critical IP and technology governance stability — contrast this with management turnover at competitor substrate companies.

Analyse the Bpifrance / CEA Investissement dual-anchor ownership: both are French state-linked institutions (Bpifrance is the French public investment bank; CEA Investissement is the investment arm of the French Atomic Energy Commission that originally developed Smart Cut™); their combined ~18.7% stake and board representation give the French state de facto veto power over major strategic decisions including M&A, capital allocation, and technology licensing; explore whether this has constrained or enabled Soitec's strategic options versus a purely privately held or US-listed peer.

Investigate the Shin-Etsu Handotai board presence: Satoshi Onishi (former SEH Europe CEO) sits on the Soitec board as a non-independent director; SEH is simultaneously a licensee of Smart Cut™ and a potential competitor in commodity SOI production; clarify the current scope of the SEH licensing agreement, whether SEH produces commodity SOI wafers using Smart Cut™ (and thus competes at the lower-value end of the market), and whether the cross-directorship creates any conflict of interest in pricing or capacity decisions.

Map the new executive team cohesion: four of nine executive committee members joined in 2023–2026 (Jeannette Schuh HR, René Jonker CPO, Albin Jacquemont CFO, Laurent Rémont CEO); compare their backgrounds against the long-tenured operators (Christophe Maleville CTO since 1993, Cyril Menon COO since 2006) to assess whether the new commercial and financial leadership has the substrate-domain knowledge required to execute the $2 billion revenue ambition.

Research the Frédéric Lissalde Chairman appointment: Lissalde's background is automotive powertrain at BorgWarner (turbochargers, eDrive systems) rather than semiconductors; his appointment in March 2025 preceded the SmartSiC impairment by eight months; explore whether his automotive OEM network was expected to accelerate SmartSiC commercial traction and whether the impairment reflects a reassessment of that thesis.

Verify director shareholding disclosures and whether Laurent Rémont received a significant equity grant upon appointment, as any performance share plan tied to the $2 billion revenue target or stock price recovery would be a meaningful alignment signal for outside investors.
